M

->**HERMETIC PHILOSOPHY**<note>original: "PHILOSOPHIA · HERMETICA"</note><-

*In the center of the page is a circular emblem. It depicts a white pelican in her "piety"—a symbolic image of a mother bird pecking her own breast to feed her young with her blood. Above the bird, golden rays of light shine down from the heavens. Beneath the nest is a white cross adorned with four red roses.*

<note>The "Pelican in her piety" is a powerful alchemical and Christian symbol. In the context of the "Great Work" of alchemy, it represents the stage of multiplication and the sacrificial nature of the philosopher who gives life to the "stone." The cross with four roses is the primary symbol of the Rosicrucians, a secret society of mystics and alchemists, representing the union of the human and the divine.</note>

# My dear reader!

Our LORD and Savior Jesus Christ, both before His suffering and after His resurrection, told His disciples—and they, as His Apostles, told the believers after His ascension—many things concerning future events, as can be seen here and there throughout the Holy Scriptures of the New Testament. Yet, within those same Scriptures, we possess no more than a single book that presents itself entirely and explicitly as prophetic; and for that very reason, because it is the only one of its kind, it is all the more significant. This is the Revelation of John, or rather, the Revelation of Jesus Christ, which He sent to John <note>The author distinguishes between the traditional title "Revelation of St. John" and the opening verse of the book itself, which describes it as "The Revelation of Jesus Christ."</note>. Now, at a time when people are least inclined to believe it, this book is beginning to become especially necessary for us and our children. Therefore, if anyone promises something toward its proper understanding and beneficial use—something that perhaps has not been observed until now—then that person, without any regard for their status, if not before others

<meta>catchword: others</meta>

<summary>The author introduces the Book of Revelation as the unique prophetic work of the New Testament, emphasizing its increasing relevance in an age of skepticism.</summary>
<keywords>Jesus Christ, Apostles, prophecy, Revelation of John, New Testament, biblical authority</keywords>

### § II.

When I had spent a considerable amount of time with the **textual criticism** <term>Critique<gloss>The scholarly study of ancient manuscripts to determine the original wording of the Bible.</gloss></term> and **interpretation** <term>Auslegung<gloss>The process of explaining the meaning of scripture, also known as exegesis.</gloss></term> of the **Greek New Testament**, and in the year 1724, in the natural course of my work, found the **Revelation** before me, I took up this book almost reluctantly. I did so only so that a major part of such a work should not be missing, and without any intention, effort, or hope of finding anything particularly special. Unexpectedly, just as I thought I was reaching the conclusion, there emerged a resolution of the **prophetic numbers** <note>original: "prophetischen Zahlen." This likely refers to the author's famous chronological calculations regarding the duration of various biblical periods, such as the 1,260 days or the number 666.</note> contained in the thirteenth and twenty-first chapters, and the great things encompassed within them. Just as little as I had previously sought this out, so little reason did I have to close my eyes to the rising light; I followed this trail, and one thing after another revealed itself. The importance and **harmony** <note>original: "Harmonie." In this context, it refers to the internal consistency and agreement between different parts of biblical prophecy.</note> of the matter itself; which occurred in those very days and continued to be [heard]...

# Preface

...resounded **Tragedy of Thorn** <note>original: "Thornische Tragödie." This refers to the "Tumult of Thorn" (1724), a significant religious conflict in the city of Toruń (Thorn) where Protestant officials were executed following a riot. It was a cause célèbre in Protestant Europe and viewed by many as a sign of the end times.</note>, whereby the blood shed upon the earth has been increased once again; my desire to agreeably compose the correspondence between **prophecy** <term>prophecy<gloss>original: "Weissagung." In this context, it refers specifically to biblical predictions concerning the fate of the Church and the world.</gloss></term> and its fulfillment moved me to communicate something to those who might assist me in one way or another, or to whom I might give some occasion for the **investigation of the truth** <note>original: "Untersuchung der Wahrheit." This reflects the author's aim to treat biblical study as a rigorous inquiry.</note>.

Since this work has now spread further than I had suspected or feared, I have become aware of the very diverse thoughts of many people—the learned and unlearned, the clever and the kind-hearted, the clerical and the secular, the pious and the coarse, the idle and the busy, the known and the foreign, the practiced and the unpracticed, those previously occupied by other opinions and those only now beginning to search; people of both sexes, every station, and every age. These thoughts, which reached me mostly by word of mouth, often in writing, and sometimes even in print, were partly favorable and modest, and partly adverse or at least timid.

This provided me with significant help in weighing many things more maturely, guarding them more carefully, and expressing them more clearly: and because the most significant...

I am nothing: if any portion of the truth has been granted to me, it has dawned upon me on the common **path to heaven** through the simple study of the **divine Word**, without my own choosing. 

I have held this dear, and according to the measure of certainty—which is often meager enough in secondary matters, but firm and clear in the fundamental core through **God’s grace**—I express it conscientiously and present it modestly for examination. ### To the First Edition

§ III. Thus, to those who are willing to accept it, there is presented (1) the entire text of the **Book of Revelation** <term>Revelation<gloss>original: "Offenbarung." The final book of the New Testament, known for its complex apocalyptic imagery.</gloss></term>, in German, in the same manner as I previously revised the entire **New Testament** in Greek according to the most reliable manuscripts <note>The author is referring to his work as a textual critic, where he compared various ancient Greek copies to establish the most accurate possible version of the biblical text.</note>. Many a person, who does not like to see new translations of the entire **New Testament** or of the **Holy Scripture**, nevertheless permits a new translation when it comes to the interpretation of individual books—for example, **Dr. Gebhardi’s** <note>Brandan Heinrich Gebhardi (1657–1729), a Lutheran theologian whose work on the twelve Minor Prophets was well-regarded at the time.</note> **twelve Minor Prophets**—and this translation of **Revelation** can, in the meantime, serve as a sample of the German translation of the entire **New Testament** which I wrote quite some time ago. I do not, however, intend to publish that full work unless there appears a reasonable hope of seeing more fruit from it than strife over it: in which case, it might come to light with a necessary explanation of the expressions that sometimes do not sound entirely German <note>The author likely refers to his attempt to stay extremely close to the original Greek syntax, which can make the German translation feel awkward or "un-German."</note>, but rather with helpful explanations of the most difficult passages and with **edifying notes** <term>edifying notes<gloss>original: "erbaulichen Anmerkungen." Annotations intended to provide spiritual encouragement and moral improvement for the reader.</gloss></term>.

# Preface

The reasons for reading the source text <term>Source Text<gloss>original: "Grund-Texte." This refers to the original Greek version of the New Testament which Bengel meticulously edited using early manuscripts.</gloss></term> in one way or another have been demonstrated elsewhere; and that much depends upon a carefully revised text—especially in the case of **Revelation**—is shown by the interpretation itself, which in many parts is only now finding its basis upon that very text. A foretaste of the interpretation is provided alongside the text itself through summary marginal glosses <term>Marginal Glosses<gloss>original: "Rand-Glossen." Brief explanatory notes printed in the margins of the page to guide the reader.</gloss></term>. (2) The detailed explanation, which consists of three parts. **7. 8. Summary of the book.**
**9. 20. John recounts how he was appointed to this important prophecy. Patmos lies in the middle of the world regions where the prophecy is fulfilled.**

VI. 1. The first four seals relate to the visible world, showing how all (1) victorious or (2) warlike times, (3) all weather, supplies, and famine, (4) all plagues of the land are within the power of the little Lamb: and a pattern of all this is given during the reign of Trajan <note>Roman Emperor Trajan, r. 98–117 AD. The author suggests that the events of the seals found a historical parallel or fulfillment during this period</note> toward the East <note>original: *Morgen*; literally "morning," a traditional term for the East</note>, West <note>original: *Abend*; literally "evening," the West</note>, South, and North.

<margin>6.</margin> These 1260 days, interpreted prophetically, are more than seven-and-a-half hundred <note>meaning 750</note> common years, and encompass the Bohemian Church <note>a reference to the pre-Reformation Christian movements in Bohemia, such as the Hussites, seen here as precursors to the later Reformation</note> from the time of Emperor Otto the Great <note>original: Ottone M. # Revelation. XII.

<margin>10</margin> * And I heard a loud voice in heaven saying: Now is come the salvation and the power, and the kingdom of our GOD, and the authority of his Anointed One: for the accuser of our brothers is cast down, who accused them before our GOD day and night. <margin>11</margin> * And they have overcome him because of the blood of the Lamb, and because of the word of their testimony, and they loved not their lives <note>original: Seele; soul or life</note> even unto death. <margin>12</margin> * Therefore rejoice, you heavens and you who dwell in them. ---

12. This Woe is the third woe. The first was brought by the angel of the abyss, and the second by the four released angels at the Euphrates: the third is stirred up by Satan himself. The "little time" amounts to $888\frac{8}{9}$ years, just as the three and a half times <note>original: viertehalb Zeiten; an archaic German expression meaning "the fourth is a half," or 3.5</note> thereafter amount to $777\frac{7}{9}$ years: these two periods of time begin one after the other and end together: into both falls the number of the Beast. This makes 42 prophetic months or $666\frac{6}{9}$ years <note>These precise fractional calculations are characteristic of 18th-century "chronological" interpretations of prophecy, which sought to map biblical "days" and "months" to exact historical years</note>. Soon after follow the 1000 years, which in the same figure are $999\frac{9}{9}$ years, just as a *Chronus* or period <note>original: Frist</note> is $111\frac{1}{9}$ years, and 2 *Chroni* make an *Aeon* <note>original: Ævum; referring to Revelation 14:6</note> or "measured eternity." The proof is in the introduction. The third woe, the three and a half times of the woman, and the times of the Beast, have long been, and still are now, in progress, and are soon hastening to an end; toward this end, that which was previously signified in Chapters 10 and 11 will also be fulfilled.

XVII, 8. The duration of the beast is divided here into three sections: I. how it was in its essence <note>original: "Esse" — Latin for "being" or "existence."</note>, during its number: II. how it is not, and how instead the woman sits upon the beast: III. how it will rage at the end as the actual man of sin and the son of perdition. ### Introduction. Sections 1 & 2.

->§ 1.<-

The prophet Daniel was commanded to shut up and seal the words given to him until the end times: Daniel 12:4, 9. In contrast, this very thing was forbidden to John much later: Revelation 22:10. Thus, despite all the length, breadth, depth, and height of its prophetic content, the **Revelation** is so constituted that we do not need other prophets to understand it; rather, we must learn to understand other prophets by means of the Revelation. This completely and orderly arranged system <note>original: "Systema"</note> carries its own key within itself. Because of its content, it is indeed uncommonly difficult; however, it also possesses a particularly easy method, as it is provided with so many joints, sections, formulas, and "handles" <note>The author uses mechanical metaphors—"Gelenke" (joints) and "Handgriffe" (handles/mechanisms)—to suggest that the text of Revelation is designed with built-in structural cues to guide the reader.</note> for its clarification.

<header>Introduction. § 3.</header>
<meta>catchword: § 4.</meta>

From this table, one can best grasp the entire contents. For in it, the content is properly broken down into its essential parts, and these are not merely arranged for some purpose of memorization. Thus, it will not be useless to compare this table with another table that follows in the first part of the conclusion.

->§ 3.<-

In the interpretation of the prophets, there has been much writing and speaking for some time now regarding so-called *hypotheses* <note>original: "Hypothesibus." In this context, the author refers to preconceived theories or frameworks that scholars often impose upon biblical prophecy before actually reading the text.</note>, which must serve as a scaffold for many, upon which they place the construction of their explanation. However, these generally flow from human whim, and the Word of God is often bent according to them, so that one brings out whatever one desires. This produces nothing good: and I strongly request that no one attribute any actually so-called hypotheses to me. One may—indeed, one must—begin only with such observations that lie clearly before one's eyes in the text; thereafter, one proceeds further and further through correct conclusions. In these observations, one may trust the text confidently, and by no means think as if the zeal of the Spirit, within which the holy John wrote, had anywhere overtaken him, and his speech had thereby been set into some disorder. In the case of imperfect men, the order of presentation suffers somewhat under great zeal; but not so with the holy men of God. Thus, we should receive that which we find before us with fine reverence, as exactly that which stands written. In a speech where your benefit or harm, honor or disgrace is at stake, self-love moves you to weigh every word very precisely; so then, the love of God will not allow you to look at the words only superficially in a prophecy that so singularly concerns God’s glory.

<summary>The author explains that his structural tables are meant for deep analysis rather than simple memorization and argues for an interpretive method based strictly on the text rather than human-made theories or "hypotheses." He asserts that the Book of Revelation is perfectly ordered by the Holy Spirit and deserves the most precise, reverent study.</summary>

<keywords>hermeneutics, hypotheses, John the Apostle, biblical order, prophetic interpretation, divine inspiration</keywords>

--- Page 134 ---
<meta>This page continues the introductory discussion on hermeneutics, moving from the rejection of preconceived "hypotheses" on the previous page to a discussion of the two primary schools of interpretation: the historical and the spiritual. It emphasizes a balanced approach that respects both the visible and invisible realms described in the Revelation of John.</meta>

<header>Introduction. § 4.</header>

->§ 4.<-

Some interpret almost everything through visible things, focusing on the history of the world and the Church; others, however, apply prophecy mostly to the invisible realm. One might call the latter a theosophical and philadelphian <note>In the 18th-century context, "Philadelphian" refers to a spiritual movement emphasizing inner piety and the "Church of Brotherly Love" described in Revelation, rather than external structures.</note>, or at least a pneumatic <note>spiritual; from the Greek 'pneuma' for spirit</note> interpretation, and the former a historical and emblematic interpretation. Both types of interpretation often do too much in their own way, and otherwise too little. # Introduction. § 10.
**II.**

...wanted to **think** <note>The syllable "ken" likely completes the word *denken* (to think) or *bemerken* (to notice) from the previous page.</note> that the prophecy begins again entirely from the start and from the top with the birth of the male child in Chapter 12:5, such an opinion is thoroughly refuted by the special, clear, and important parallelism between the voices in Chapter 11:15 and the voice in Chapter 12:10. Those former voices say: *The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ.* And afterwards, this later voice says: *Now have come the salvation, and the power, and the kingdom of our God, and the authority of His Christ.* Those voices undeniably belong under the **trumpet of the seventh angel**; therefore, this voice also necessarily belongs under that same trumpet. For the matter is entirely the same, with only this distinction: that in this voice, through the word "now" (<note>original Greek: *arti* (αρτι)</note>), the outcome is recorded even more specifically and sharply, and is praised more extensively through the accompanying words. From this, it can be seen all the more clearly that those voices precede this voice, and thus this one belongs just as certainly as the others under the trumpet of the seventh angel. Indeed, between those voices and this one falls the actual beginning of the **execution** <note>The practical carrying out or fulfillment of the divine decree.</note> of this trumpet, when Satan is cast out of heaven. Everything that happens after this fall is interconnected.

From these three remarks, the following conclusions now arise:

**I.** Of that which stands in Chapter 10:1 to 11:13, nothing belongs to the **second woe**.

This flows from the first remark and is further proven by the following contrast: in the second woe, the result is a terrible lack of repentance (Chapter 11:20–21 <note>The author likely refers to Revelation 9:20–21, which describes the unrepentant survivors of the sixth trumpet/second woe, as Chapter 11 does not have 20 verses.</note>); whereas in Chapter 11:13, at the fulfillment of the **mystery of God** <note>The ultimate realization of God's hidden plan for salvation and history.</note>, it results in the conversion of a very great multitude. However, the end of the second woe and the beginning of what is written from Chapter 10:1 to 11:13 continue alongside each other in time for a while.

**II.** The **third woe** is described in detail in Chapter 13, and is preliminarily announced in Chapter 12:12 <note>Revelation 12:12: "Woe to the inhabiters of the earth and of the sea! for the devil is come down unto you, having great wrath."</note>.

| 1st Woe: | 2nd Woe: | [3rd Woe:] |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1. Occasion:** A star that fell from heaven and opens the shaft of the abyss: | The one who calls from the horns of the golden altar: "Release the four angels at the Euphrates": | Michael, after whose victory the dragon is cast out of heaven. |

| **5. Duration:** <term>Währung</term> <note>Literally "currency," but used here in the archaic sense of the "validity" or "duration" of a specific period.</note> five months: | Hour, day, month, year: | A short time, 42 months, etc. |
| **6. Power:** To torment, without death: | To kill: | All manner of calamity. |

Here stand three columns side-by-side, and six points one after another. In the first column is the first woe, and in the second is the second woe. Let everyone consider whether it is possible—given that the third column is similar to the first and second in every point, yet even more terrifying—that one should fail to see a "woe" there? Should one not rather recognize this very thing as the third, and indeed the greatest, woe? 

However, there are even more considerations to add, as the third woe shares similarities partly with the first and second simultaneously, or (for reasons that will appear in the commentary) with only one of them; in other respects, it possesses its own unique characteristics as the most severe of all. ->§ 11.<-

### Introduction. § 13.

...which the following letters, seals, trumpets, and bowls cover; where people seek a consistently equal length for such periods of time, but occasionally interpret the letters or the bowls elsewhere. The **three woes** <term>Three Woes: The final three judgments signaled by the last three trumpets in Revelation 8:13, 9:12, and 11:14</term> have their own durations, but of an unequal and ever-increasing length: and in between there are two intervals, which must be regarded just as much as periods of time <note>original Latin: "Periodos temporum"</note> (just as pauses also belong to a piece of music); although their actual length is as little expressed as the length of the trumpets of the first, second, third, and fourth angels, of which it is not specifically indicated whether one ends earlier or later, or at the same time as another begins. 

Conversely, under the single trumpet of the seventh angel, many long periods of time <note>original Latin: "Periodi temporum"</note> are contained entirely within Chapters 10–20. For this reason, it is not at all accurately stated when people speak of "seven periods of time" even in relation to the trumpets, since they are rather seven judgments, visitations, etc., which indeed occur one after another, but also have many other time periods between and after them—some more tolerable, others more joyful. And why should the span from John on Patmos <note>John of Patmos: The traditional author of the Book of Revelation, who received his visions while in exile on the Greek island of Patmos.</note> to the end of all things be divided into seven periods of time, any more than the times of the **Old Testament** separately, or the times of the **Old and New Testaments** together? 

Regarding the seven churches and their angels, the seven seals, and the seven bowls, one is even less authorized to create seven periods of time. For although the seven trumpets constitute seven time periods, it does not follow that the churches, the seals, and the bowls—simply because there are also seven of each—also aim at seven periods of time; otherwise, the seven horns of the **Lamb** <term>The Lamb: A central symbolic image of Jesus Christ in the Book of Revelation, representing sacrifice and ultimate victory</term>, the seven thunders, etc., would also have to yield seven periods of time. ### Introduction. § 14. 15.

...that everything which, according to the Revelation, is to happen, should happen quickly—except for that which is expressly enclosed in lengthy periods of time. ### § 17.

These four **spheres** or districts relate to one another in such a way that, in one's interpretation, one can not only remain safely within the order of the text, but one must necessarily remain there. (p. 199 f.) It is an error when one divides the book in such a way that this or that part runs until the end of the world, and then the following part is supposed to start again from the beginning with the first times of the New Testament. Consider § 10 and 13. First come the addresses to the seven churches and their angels, immediately thereafter the seven seals, and just as soon, with the seventh seal, the seven trumpets; but finally, only under the trumpet of the seventh angel, do the seven bowls begin.

# Introduction. § 18.
F 2
<meta>catchword: About</meta>

->§ 18.<-

Yet this is not to be understood as if every part in such an **order** must be completely fulfilled before the fulfillment of the following part begins; otherwise, it would not have been necessary for this to be specifically noted regarding the **three woes**: Chapter IX:12, XI:14. <note>These verses in Revelation mark the conclusion of specific "woe" judgments, signaling the transition from one catastrophic event to the next.</note> Thus, it does not follow that the **letters** <note>The seven epistles to the churches in Asia Minor found in Revelation 2–3.</note> must all be entirely finished before the **seals** are opened: that the opened **seals** must be fully carried out before the **trumpets** begin: or that even the seventh **trumpet** must be entirely over before the **bowls** are poured out. It does not proceed step by step, from one little verse to the next; rather, the point is only that the **beginning** of each part precedes the **beginning** of the following part.

The **letters** begin before the **seals**, the **seals** before the **trumpets**, the **trumpets** before the **bowls**. One **letter** begins before another, one **seal** before another, one **trumpet** (primarily) before another, and one **bowl** before another. In this manner, something can stand earlier in the text without disrupting the order, yet its outcome may follow much later. A remarkable example has already occurred in § 10. Indeed, that which starts later sometimes ends sooner: and that which starts earlier may also extend beyond the later part. The **bowls** only begin under the trumpet of the seventh **angel**, and they soon pass away, after which that same trumpet shows its power anew. The **seals** begin before the **trumpet**, and even after the seventh angel had already been sounding for a long time, the fifth **seal**, for example, still demonstrates its effect when the longing of the souls under the altar is fulfilled: Chapter XIX:2. <note>The "souls under the altar" from the fifth seal (Rev 6:9) cry out for justice, which the author sees finally answered much later during the judgment of Babylon.</note> The **letters** precede the **seals**; and in the first **letter**, the eating from the **Tree of Life** is promised, which finally comes to light with and within the **New Jerusalem**: which then perfectly agrees with the contents of the letters, seals, trumpets, and bowls indicated in § 14.

### § 19.

Anyone who has recognized such an order also finds themselves at home in the beautiful *Simultaneum* <note>original: "Simultaneum"; a term used here to describe events happening at the same time or a literary technique where narratives overlap.</note>, or in the elegant manner of the text, where often of two things that belong precisely to the same time, one is divided into two parts and, as it were, split open, and the other is unexpectedly placed between those two parts, *per parenthesin* <note>original: "per parenthesin"; meaning "as a parenthesis" or an insertion.</note>. Thus, the following meet together: those in the white robes and all the angels: Chapter VII:9, 10: 11, 12: 13-17. The conversation of the Elder with John, and the angelic business: v. 11, 12: 13-17: VIII:2. The trumpet of the seven angels and the incense-burning of another angel: Chapter VIII:2. (3. 4. 5.) 6. The oath of the mighty angel and the seven thunders: Chapter X:3. (4) 5. The fall of the dragon to the earth and the song of praise in heaven: Chapter XII:9. (10-12.) 13. The heavenly voice and the speech of the Spirit: Chapter XIV:13. The seven angels with the seven last plagues, and the song of praise at the glassy sea, as well as the temple filled with smoke from the glory of God: Chapter XV. The duties of the sixth angel with the bowl, the departure of the three unclean spirits, and the encouragement to vigilance: likewise the bowl of the seventh angel together with its result, and in between the word, "It is done": Chapter XVI:12-18. The rejoicing of the saints and the angels over Babylon's <note>In the Book of Revelation, Babylon is often interpreted as a symbolic representation of a corrupt worldly power or city opposed to God.</note> judgment: Chapter XVIII:20. (21-23.) 24. Babylon’s judgment and smoke, and in between the Hallelujah: Chapter XIX:2. (3.) 3. The release of Satan and the first resurrection: Chapter XX:3. (4-6.) 7. John's word, "Come," and the Lord Jesus's word, "I come," Chapter XXII:20. To this can be added Chapter II and III, the phrase, "He who has an ear," as this is placed three times before and four times after the promise, "He who overcomes," and thus proceeds alongside the same. See also Chapter II:10, III:8, XXI:5, 6.

->§ 20.<-

The seven seals, the seven trumpets, and the seven bowls are consistently divided into groups of four and three. For example, the first four seals have a special connection with one another, as do the last three. For with each of the first four seals, there is always a heavenly creature <note>original: "himmlisches Thier"; referring to the "four living creatures" described in Revelation 4 and 6.</note> who calls for John to "come," as well as a horse of a specific color and a rider with certain insignia. With the last three seals, however, there is neither one nor the other. The trumpets of the last three angels bring three "Woes" along with many other circumstances (§ 10.) that are not found with the first four trumpets. Furthermore, these first four—much like the bowls of the first four angels—affect the earth, the sea, the rivers, and the sun; however, the trumpets and bowls of the last three angels are directed elsewhere. In the seven letters <note>original: "Sendschreiben"; the seven letters to the churches in Asia Minor.</note>, a division into four and three (or three and four) can also be observed. But because these letters have their own special character, this is not as easily considered here in the introduction as it is in the commentary (Chapter III:22). This classification is clear, important, and useful.

->§ 21.<-

The Group of Four, as will be demonstrated in the commentary, refers to the four quarters of the world. Under the first four seals, the Lion faces the East <note>original: "gegen Morgen"; literally "towards the morning."</note>, the Calf faces the West <note>original: "gegen Abend"; literally "towards the evening."</note>, the Man faces the South <note>original: "gegen Mittag"; literally "towards midday."</note>, and the Eagle faces the North <note>original: "gegen Mitternacht"; literally "towards midnight."</note>. Similarly, with the trumpets and bowls: the "earth" indicates Asia; the "sea" indicates Europe; and the "rivers" (or the trees standing beside them) indicate Africa. The "sun" has all of these, including the northern regions, lying beneath it. Ecclesiastes I:3.

In particular, however, the seventh is always the most significant—or even more important than the previous six combined. For under the seventh seal <term>seal: the divine judgments in Revelation are revealed by breaking seven seals on a scroll</term> are the seven trumpets, and under the trumpet of the seventh angel, alongside many other things, the seven bowls are contained. And so, too, the bowl of the seventh angel surpasses the bowls of the preceding angels.

->§ 25.<-

For this reason, there is always a preparation that precedes the seventh, as it is the most important. The preparation for the seventh seal <note>The seventh seal is unique because it contains the entirety of the next sequence of judgments—the trumpets.</note> occurs through the sealing of the 144,000 (Chapter 7). The preparation for the trumpet of the seventh angel occurs through a solemn oath, etc. <note>original: "2c."; an archaic abbreviation for et cetera.</note> (Chapters 10 and 11). The preparation for the bowl of the seventh angel happens through a call to watchfulness (Chapter 16:15). Therefore, these should not actually be seen as parts of the sixth seal, or of the trumpet and bowl of the sixth angel. In each sixth element, the narrative is, as it were, broken off, and then completed in the seventh.

Introduction. § 28.

Text points to the Chaldeans, so specifically the Hebrew words Abaddon, Satan, Accuser <note>original: "Katigor"; a Hebrew transliteration of the Greek "katēgoros", often used in rabbinic literature to describe the prosecuting counsel or accuser</note>, Amen, Hallelujah, etc., point to the Hebrews. The history of the people of Israel makes up almost everything in the Old Testament: but since the times of Titus and Hadrian <note>referring to the Roman Emperors who suppressed the Jewish revolts and destroyed Jerusalem in 70 AD and 135 AD</note> it is barely included as an incidental matter. No one can do without it less than an interpreter of Revelation. This prophecy extends from the old Jerusalem destroyed by the Romans to the new Jerusalem: and thus this holy people of Israel is of such a distinction (Chapter 11:1), which even extends into eternity, Chapter 21:12, 24. The Apostle to the Gentiles himself explains everywhere that the Gentiles are only fellow-sharers <note>original: "Mitgenossen"</note> of Israel. In Asia there were many Israelites in particular, who were first converted by Paul and afterwards strengthened by Peter's letters from Babylon, Acts 19:1, 1 Peter 1:1. Thus, among these seven congregations in Asia, the first foundation was from Israel, and they were especially under John's supervision. Lightfoot writes quite elegantly in *Hours* <note>original: "Horis", referring to John Lightfoot's "Horae Hebraicae et Talmudicae", a scholarly work explaining the New Testament through Jewish tradition</note> on 1 Corinthians, page 270: James, Peter, and John went to the circumcision <note>a biblical idiom for those preaching to the Jews</note>, and to each one his diocese can well be assigned. James received Palestine and Syria: Peter received Babylon and Assyria: John received the Hellenists <note>Greek-speaking Jews</note>, primarily in Asia and further beyond. Therefore, Asia was so convenient that John should send the Revelation there. In Patmos, he had Asia and the land of Israel in his vision at the same time. To the conversion of Israel, this book will contribute greatly in its time, when Israel recognizes what is still reserved for them by virtue of this book. Whoever has the ability and opportunity to apply this proof correctly, let them do so.

If we now apply the prophecy to our present time, we must take the following points to heart.

Should someone object that in Scripture, a day often signifies a year—citing Numbers 14:33–34, Ezekiel 4:5–6, Daniel 9:24–26, and Luke 13:33—this is the answer: The fourth of these passages deals with natural days, as is noted in the *Harmony of the Evangelists* § 126. The third does not belong here, for the word "day" does not appear there; rather, the "week" signifies, directly, seven complete years. In the second passage, a year is merely represented by a day; and in the first, a year of punishment is established for each day of sin. It does not say: "Your children shall wander in the wilderness for forty days (that is, forty years)." Nowhere does the word "day" stand in place of the word "year," as Patrick Forbes <note>original: "Patricius Forbesius"—referring to the Scottish bishop and scholar Patrick Forbes (1564–1635), known for his commentary on the Apocalypse.</note> recognized long ago in his work on the Apocalypse, page 85. Also, Revelation 21 uses a different measure than Ezekiel 40.

but one should also not shrink back under a pretense of humility, but rather allow oneself to be enticed and attracted by such important words—following with reverent desire as far as one finds the door and the path open. We therefore make the following observations with all possible clarity:

I. A number is attributed to the Beast and to his name.

It is enough for now that 666 is the number of the Beast itself, which is presented here not merely to be numbered <note>original: *numeriren*; to simply count or identify the digits.</note> or counted, but is set as a task to be calculated <note>original: *calculiren*; implying a deeper mathematical or chronological deduction.</note>.

IV. When one is to have a complete concept of a number, two terms belong to it: namely, an **adjective** and a **substantive**. For example: "twelve apostles." Here, "twelve" is the counting number <note>original: *numerus numerans*; the abstract numeral or digit.</note>, and the total of the apostles is the counted number <note>original: *numerus numeratus*; the actual quantity of people.</note>. For the sake of distinction, we shall call the former a **numeral** <note>original: *Zifferzahl*.</note> and the latter a **quantity** <note>original: *Anzahl*.</note> for a short while.

V. Where both are found together, no calculation is necessary.

VI. But where, as is the case here, a calculation is required, then either the unknown **numeral** belonging to a known **quantity** is found through such calculation: for example, one who undertakes a large building project knows beforehand that a quantity of dollars will be required; but how many hundreds or thousands of dollars he needs, he must investigate, and that is what is called "calculating" in Luke 14:28. <note>Luke 14:28: "For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?"</note>

VII. Or, the **quantity** which is still unknown is found through calculation based on the **numeral** which is known.

VIII. Here, the **numeral** is expressly given as 666, and to that extent, it does not first need to be brought to light through a calculation.

For **I.** the word **number** is often used when speaking of times: and in the <note>The Aramaic phrase "Mene, Mene, Tekel, Upharsin" from Daniel 5:25, which translates to "Numbered, numbered, weighed, and divided."</note> *Numbered, Numbered* <note>original: *Mene Mene*</note> it signifies the times of Belshazzar's reign, just as in Chapter XVII. 10. the numeral *a little* <note>original Greek: *ὀλίγον* (oligon)</note> means a little (time). **II.** From the ninth chapter onwards, the intervals of time are frequently expressed doubly, as we noted in § 26. Num. IV. Thus, it will also be found in the highly significant times of the Beast.

**XVII.** In the entire description of the Beast, no other numbers appear except the **10 horns**, the **7 heads**, and the **42 months**. In similarity with the horns and heads, the Beast would have to have 666 pieces that somehow belonged to its body. In similarity with the 42 months, the **number of the Beast** must yield 666 times. The former contradicts the idiom, *number of the Beast*, and is also not probable for the reason that in the Beast—which we shall find in Chapter XIII. 1. to be a **spiritual and worldly power**—one will not be able to find 666 parts to consider. Thus, only the latter remains, namely the 42 months, which, as we intended after the beginning of this 43rd §, also require a resolution and find it nowhere but here.

->XVIII.<-

**XVIII.** Therefore, we may say: The 42 months are times; therefore the 666 are also times. Thus, it remains a matter of comparing the 42 months and the number of the Beast.

**XIX.** These two <term>periods of time</term> <note>original: *Zeitläuffe*; refers to the flow or course of time across a specific interval</note> do not flow one after the other—in which case neither of the two could be compared with the other through <term>calculation</term> <note>original: *Calculation*; the process of interpreting biblical numbers to find historical dates</note>—but rather alongside one another, just like the other pair of time periods just cited. **XX.** The 666 are human times, or times customary in human life, namely common days or years <term>etc.</term> <note>original: *2c.*; an archaic abbreviation for *et cetera*</note>. On the other hand, the 42 months of the Beast are not called human months, one of which has about 30 natural days: and we have already proven in § 40 that they are <term>prophetic months</term>. <note>In historicist prophecy, a "prophetic" unit often differs from a "human" unit (for example, the day-year principle where one day equals one year).</note>

**XXI.** The 42 months and the number 666 are two equal periods of time. Otherwise, one could not find a firm footing in the so clearly commanded calculation. This equality will be further proven with more detail in § 47.

### Introduction. § 43.

XXVII. Whoever holds the Vulgate <note>The Latin translation of the Bible, which the Catholic Church declared the official version at the Council of Trent</note> in as high regard as the Council of Trent <note>An ecumenical council held between 1545 and 1563</note> prescribes, cannot avoid the conclusion that he must understand the number as 666 years. For this translation has, from of old, not used *six hundred* <note>original: "sexcenta" — a neuter form</note> etc., but rather *six hundred sixty-six* <note>original: "sexcenti sexaginta sex" — a masculine form</note> in the masculine: whereby in Latin, a masculine noun must necessarily be understood, and it will be difficult to find anything else suitable to fill that role other than *years* <note>Latin: "anni"</note>. If the Vulgate is meant to have an error here, it is a very significant error.

XXVIII. The times of the Beast stand in contrast to the measurements of the New Jerusalem, which is described thus: *And the angel measured the city with the rod at 12,000 stadiums. Its length and breadth and height are equal. And he measured its wall, 144 measures of a human, which is that of an angel* Chapter XXI. 16. 17. At that specific passage, we intend to provide the interpretation and its proof; here, however, we only mention how both passages relate to each other in so many ways.

1) There stands a pair of numbers, namely 12,000 and 144. Here also, namely 42 and 666.

2) There is an <term>ellipsis</term> <note>A grammatical term for when words are omitted because they are understood from context</note>; here too, in that with the 144, just as many <term>measuring rods</term> <note>original: "Calami" or "Meßruthen"</note> (see clearly the *Gnomon* <note>Referring to Johann Albrecht Bengel’s famous New Testament commentary, 'Gnomon Novi Testamenti'</note> on Apocalypse XXI. 17) are to be understood, and with the 666, just as many years are to be understood.

3) In both places it is indicated of what kind the measuring rods and years are. Those are angelic-human; these, however, are a pure <term>human number</term> <note>original: "Menschenzahl"</note>. Those are measured out by an angel appearing in human form; these are calculated by human understanding.

4) There, the 12,000 stadiums are not of the same kind as the 144 angelic-human measuring rods, but rather, by virtue of the contrast, only human or common stadiums; for without this contrast, 144 measuring rods would relate to 12,000 stadiums of the same kind like an inch to the height of a tower: and thus here also, the number 666 consists of human

### § 52.

With this, we have discussed the time spans <term>Time spans (German: *Zeitläuffe*) refers to the chronological intervals or durations within the author's prophetic system.</term> found in the text, and we have not even been concerned with what a single prophetic day or month, or hour or year, actually is by itself: such a question is not even necessary for us. For none of these simple units of time stands alone in the text. We have derived the prophetic month and day to the extent that the former is, roughly, 15 to 16 common years, and the latter is, roughly, half of a common year. Before I noticed the important relationship of the number 666 to the 1,000 years, the length of the half-year, as signified by a prophetic day, could not be precisely determined: therefore, the *Sketch* <note>original: "Grundriß"; referring to the author's earlier work, *Grundriß der prophetischen Zeitrechnung* (1740).</note> on pages 26 and 45 was arranged no differently than precisely on the basis of a half-year; yet even so, by virtue of what was already reported in the *Sketch* itself in § 22, and now in this Introduction in § 38-42, it was impossible to have erred very far.

Now, hopefully, the even closer determination of the prophetic day, and that which depends upon it, will be even more favorably received, especially since it is now intended to remain fixed. It is the half-year or <term>Semester <gloss>original: *Semestre*</gloss></term>, which, precisely or roughly, is already a complete and significant unit of time in its own measure—not indeed in all languages, but certainly in astronomy, in <term>Civil Law <gloss>original: *Jure civili*</gloss></term>, in common human life, and even among the Hebrews, who had the New Year in the autumn and the first month in the spring, etc. <note>The Hebrew calendar has both a religious start (Nisan in Spring) and a civil start (Tishrei in Autumn), effectively splitting the year into two six-month halves.</note> <term>Theodoret</term> <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393 – c. 458 AD) was an influential theologian and biblical commentator of the school of Antioch.</note> in his <term>Commentary on Daniel 4:13 <gloss>original: *comm. IV. 13.*</gloss></term> interprets the "seven times" as so many winters or summers—which would be seven <term>semesters</term>—and in doing so, he refers to other interpreters. <term>Thomas Parker</term> <note>Thomas Parker (1595–1677) was a Puritan minister and scholar who emigrated to New England; his commentary on Daniel was published in 1646.</note> in his <term>Commentary on Daniel <gloss>original: *comm. Dan.*</gloss></term> explains the 2,300 days in <term>Chapter 8:14 <gloss>original: *Cap. VIII. 14.*</gloss></term> as so many halves, or 1,150 whole years. Finally, various peoples in Asia, Europe, and Africa—among whom Patmos <note>The island where the Apostle John received the visions of the Book of Revelation.</note> was situated nearby and in the center—in ancient times counted every six months as a year.

# Introduction. § 53.

We have taken the **1,000 years** to be ordinary years, and yet, for example, we have taken the **42 months** of the **Beast** to be prophetic months. Will it not be further argued: should not all such periods of time be understood either entirely in a prophetic sense, or entirely in an ordinary sense?

This objection appears plausible, and those who defend the "year-day" principle <note>The "year-day" principle is a method of interpretation where each "day" mentioned in prophecy represents one solar year.</note>—as well as all those who do not use the **Number of the Beast** as a chronological aid—will find it difficult to escape this point. Consequently, some have felt a hesitation as to whether the **1,000 years** should not also be resolved into days, and each such day be taken for a year. This idea is rightly rejected, and indeed must be rejected, if one were to take each of those days at even an average measurement. For the **1,000 years** precede the end of the world, and even precede **Gog and Magog**; and certainly, at the time of Christ’s suffering, the world was no longer at the beginning of its lifespan, but had already passed the midpoint. It is hard to imagine that the world should still have over 360,000 or 180,000 years left to stand.

However, the words for <term>day</term> <note>original Greek: *hēmera*</note> and <term>month</term> <note>original Greek: *mēn*</note> are used in both prophetic and ordinary senses. Nevertheless, such a distinction is not to be entirely overlooked, as two different types of years also bring with them two types of proportional months and days.

# Revelation — To John. I. 1.

...brought forth. Those books the Apostles and Evangelists, like their oral sermons and speeches, produced mostly out of the rich treasure of wisdom and knowledge residing within them, whenever and wherever they saw fit under the impulse of the Spirit of Christ. To write the **Revelation**, however, **John** was given a quite special command and new **instruction** <note>original: *Instruction*; here meaning a formal set of orders or a specific mandate for a divine task.</note> after he had led the **apostolic office** for some sixty years. JESUS Christ dictated His Revelation to John: and the book is not John’s, but JESUS Christ’s. This is why, although John uses so many lovely titles in his letters—*my little children*, *you beloved*, *my brothers*—he refrains from them throughout this entire book. He does not write for himself, but in the name of JESUS Christ.

-># Revelation — to John. I. 1.<-

**IV. John remained until the Lord's coming.**

This is evident from the preceding notes. If the brothers had said: "**This disciple does not die until the Lord comes**," they would have, in a certain sense, spoken correctly. However, they believed this limitation to be unnecessary; they thought that if John were to remain until the Lord came, he would not die at all, but rather that the Lord would find him alive on the Last Day <term>Last Day: The final day of the world and the time of the last judgment</term>.

**V. The coming of Christ, of which we speak here, is understood not according to its final fulfillment on the Last Day, but according to its beginning.**

When Jesus rose from the dead, he spoke that very same morning of his ascension; and indeed, because it was to happen soon after, in forty days, he did not say: "**I will ascend**," but rather, "**I am ascending**" <note>Referring to John 20:17: "I am ascending to my Father and your Father."</note>: just as he had also counted his suffering itself as part of this journey to the Father. John 14:4. 2. However, the text says, *who testified*, not *who testifies*. This is because it was the custom of the ancients to often direct the words in their writings and books not toward the time of the writing, but toward the time of the reading <note>This grammatical convention is known as the "epistolary past," where a writer uses the past tense to describe actions that are current to them but will be in the past by the time the letter reaches the recipient.</note>. *I, Paul, am writing this with my own hand*, is how it might have been said in Philemon v. 19, since Paul was writing from Rome; but by the time Philemon read the letter in Asia <note>Referring to the Roman province of Asia, in modern-day Turkey</note>, it became, *I, Paul, have written it*. Thus, while John was writing on Patmos, it might have been said, *he testifies*; but when the book was read in Asia, it was said, *he has testified*. And in verse 3, it does not say *what is being written*, but rather *what is written*. In this way, this second verse connects clearly with the first and third.

¶ **The Word of GOD and the Testimony of JESUS CHRIST)** It says the same in verse 9, and not much differently in chapter 12:17 and 14:12. **The Word of GOD**, John says here—just as the ancient prophets often said—is **the Word of the LORD**. **The Testimony of JESUS CHRIST** is the witness which **JESUS** Christ, as the faithful witness, allows to come to us. Let no one be ashamed of this word and testimony (2 Timothy 1:8, 2:9).

¶ **He who reads and those who hear**) Why not "he who reads and he who hears," or "those who read and those who hear"? And why is it phrased this way: **he who reads** (as one person) and **those who hear** (as many)? The discussion here is not about someone reading for themselves in silence—which is certainly appropriate for everyone—but rather about someone who reads it aloud in a public assembly so that many may hear it [Rev 22:17, 18]. 

John was confined and banished to the island of Patmos by pagan persecution; he was not permitted to go into Asia <note>In the New Testament, "Asia" refers to the Roman province of Proconsular Asia, located in modern-day western Turkey.</note> at that time, and so he was commanded to send this book to Asia. Now, such a precious scripture could not be entrusted to just anyone who happened to come along. Rather, just as the Apostolic Church (and the various congregations within it, even those located far apart) maintained the most precise correspondence, and many upright people considered it an honor to serve as **messengers for the saints** <note>original: *Briefträger der Heiligen* — literally "letter-carriers of the holy ones," referring to the trusted individuals who carried epistles between early Christian communities</note>; so too here, a righteous disciple of John showed his service by bringing the book across from Patmos into Asia.

Observ.* — refers to John Gregory’s *Observationes* (1646), drawing from Arabic historical sources</note>—or some other name, he had more to do than just deliver the scroll. # I. 4. John — Throne.

After the death of Paul or other Apostles who had been in Asia, other congregations were, so to speak, left orphaned; and it was upon these seven—which Tertullian <note>Tertullian (c. 155 – c. 220 AD) was a prolific early Christian author from Carthage.</note> in his fourth book against Marcion, chapter 5, calls *alumnas Joannis* <note>original: "alumnas Joannis" — John's foster children or nursing-children.</note>—that the Apostolic Church now depended. John, who was deemed worthy for this great Revelation to pass through his hand, had a close acquaintance and much interaction with these seven congregations or their angels <note>In the context of Revelation, the "angels" of the churches are usually interpreted as the bishops or presiding leaders of those specific Christian communities.</note> during his time in Asia, as is especially known regarding the congregation at Ephesus. From these, the book later spread to many other intervening Asian cities and into all the surrounding Christian world.

<meta>catchword: ¶ They</meta>

By order of the Lord himself, he addresses the angels of the congregations. Each congregation <note>original: *Gemeine* — This term refers to the local community of believers or "church."</note> and its angel had a precise connection and similarity with one another, yet they were also distinguished from each other to a certain extent. <margin>v. 20.</margin> To the congregations, he must send the book; to their angels, he must write.

¶ **To Ephesus, etc.**) The seven cities appear again in this exact order hereafter in chapters II and III. An Englishman, Thomas Smith, traveled through these seven cities in 22 days in the year 1671 and published a description of them. According to his account, it is 46 (English) miles from Ephesus to Smyrna, 64 from Smyrna to Pergamum, 48 from Pergamum to Thyatira, 33 from Thyatira to Sardis, 27 from Sardis to Philadelphia, and about 42 miles from Philadelphia to Laodicea. The total would be 260 English, or 52 German miles <note>A German mile (*Deutsche Meile*) was much longer than an English mile, roughly equivalent to 4.6 miles or 7.5 kilometers.</note>. These cities lie in Ionia, Mysia, and Lydia, all within Asia, insofar as this was reckoned as a Roman province. The journey of the reader commissioned by John went mostly from the West and North toward the South and East <note>original: *von Abend und Mitternacht gegen Mittag und Morgen* — In archaic German, "Evening" and "Midnight" refer to West and North, while "Midday" and "Morning" refer to South and East.</note>.

<header>II. 1. To the Angel — Lampstand.</header>

I. These seven letters are of great importance. Just as the people of Israel had to sanctify themselves when the Law was to be given to them, and just as John <note>referring to John the Baptist</note> had to preach the baptism of repentance when the Kingdom of Heaven drew near, so too must the Christian congregation and its leaders prepare themselves through repentance and steadfastness to worthily receive this great Revelation. Therefore, whoever wishes to handle this precious book correctly must, above all else, follow the exhortations found in these seven letters. In the same way, Israel must be ashamed of all its evil deeds when the dwelling of God and its arrangement is shown to them. <note>original: "Ez. XLIII. 10. 11."; a reference to the prophet Ezekiel being told to describe the Temple to the Israelites so they might feel shame for their sins.</note>

II. These letters still belong to the introduction of the book. They serve as a sevenfold preface to the work, or a preparation for the subject matter itself. Here, the Savior appears in human form, and not yet under the image of a little Lamb <note>original: "Lämmlein"; a term of endearment and theological significance in 18th-century German Pietism, referring to Christ's sacrificial nature which becomes the primary motif starting in Revelation chapter 5.</note>. He speaks mostly in literal terms, and not yet so figuratively. It is only in chapter 4, verse 1, that John sees the opened door in heaven, and in verse 2 he says: **I was in the Spirit**, just as he had stated in chapter 1, verse 10. This phrase is not repeated again throughout the entire book because everything that follows, from Chapter 4 to 22, remains connected as a single, continuous discourse. The entire vision <term>vision; original: "Gesicht"; refers to a supernatural revelation or prophetic sight</term> was experienced by John at a single time, on a single day, in two distinct parts: first, Chapters 1–3; and afterward, Chapters 4–22.

<meta>This page continues the structural analysis of the seven letters to the seven churches in Revelation. Having previously established the importance of these letters as a preparation for the prophecy, the author now breaks down the specific four-part template used in each letter.</meta>

<page-num>219</page-num>
<header>To the Angel—Lampstand. II. 1.</header>
<meta>catchword: the</meta>

III. The structure of the seven letters is consistent throughout; for in each one there is:
1. A command to write to an angel <note>referring to the leader or presiding minister</note> of a congregation.
2. A glorious **Title of Jesus Christ**.
3. An address to the angel of the congregation, which contains:
	1. A testimony of its current state—whether mixed, good, or evil.
	2. An exhortation to repentance or to steadfastness.
	3. An announcement of what shall happen, most especially concerning the coming of the Lord.
4. A promise for the one who overcomes, along with the awakening word: **He who has an ear** *etc.*

These two terms, Address and Promise, we shall have to use frequently; therefore one should keep well in mind what is understood by each. The Address in each letter consists more of clear, literal words; in the Promise, however, the Spirit speaks more with figurative <note>original: "verblümten"; literally "flowery," meaning symbolic or metaphorical</note> language that reappears in the following main vision <note>referring to the prophetic visions starting in chapter 4</note>. In the Address, the Lord Jesus speaks primarily and first to those congregations then in Asia <note>referring to the Roman province of Asia, in modern-day Turkey</note> by name, and specifically to their angels: the Promise speaks in the *third person* <note>original: "tertia persona"</note> of those who overcome in those first times and also in the times to follow, and imparts to them a share in the

anticipated extract of the precious promises from the final chapters of the book, which are granted to them after victory in that world, both before and after the end of this world.

Thus, the seven letters begin from a high vantage point and reach very far into the future, although the description of Christ, who is the First and the Last, begins even earlier in chapter 1 and reaches even further, even to the very conclusion of the book.

Further details concerning the seven letters in general follow immediately in the commentary on the letter to the angel of the congregation at Ephesus, as well as at Chapter III:22.

¶ **Angel**) We noted at chapter I:20 that this was not Timothy, who by then had nearly reached the end of his life. This "angel" <note>referring to the presiding minister or bishop of the church</note> may have entered his office not long before the date the Revelation was given.

¶ **To Ephesus**) One can compare what is reported of this congregation from the time of Paul onward in Acts 19 and 20, and here and there in Paul's letters. John himself returned to Ephesus from Patmos <note>the island where John was exiled and received his visions</note>.

¶ **Write**) Thus, JESUS Christ dictated these letters to John word for word.

¶ **Thus says**) A magnificent and majestic introduction! It is exactly what occurs so often in the Old Testament: "Thus says the LORD" <note>original Hebrew: נאם (*ne’um*), a prophetic declaration</note>.

¶ **He who holds**) The seven titles of Jesus Christ in these seven letters are very magnificent. See Chapter II:1, 8, 12, 18 and III:1, 7, 14. Consider them one after another in the text itself.

|---|---|

Thus, in this table, the explanation for the first three points stands opposite them in the last three.

¶ **That you cannot bear those who are evil**) Patience, and earnestness against the wicked, sit well together.

<header>And you have — become. II. 3.</header>
<meta>catchword: The</meta>

...excluded from the fellowship of Christ <note>The text begins mid-word with "-meinschaft," completing "Gemeinschaft" (fellowship/communion) from the previous page</note>. The necessity of struggle and being good—or at least possessing something good—go hand in hand. We see this not only in the church at Smyrna, but also in Ephesus, etc. The churches at Sardis and Laodicea had no one to struggle against; yet the latter was wretched, and the former was dead.

¶ **And they are not**) This shows that it was still the apostolic age; otherwise, there could no longer have been false apostles. Among the qualities required of an apostle was that he must have seen the Lord Jesus personally. Therefore, false apostles (referencing 2 Corinthians 11:13) were those who not only promoted false doctrine but also adorned it with an apostolic authority, whether they had actually seen the Lord Jesus or merely falsely claimed to have done so.

¶ **And have found them to be liars**) Many people might have judged the leader <term>Vorsteher: the presiding officer or pastor of the congregation</term> of this church to be a harsh and quarrelsome man for refusing to tolerate people who did not seem entirely rejectable. But the Lord praises him. Truth is something pure and delicate.

¶ **You have borne**) Reference to 2 Timothy 2:24 <note>The verse cited discusses how a servant of the Lord must be patient and able to endure evil</note>.

<header>II. 4. But — you have left.</header>
<meta>catchword: ¶ Re-</meta>

### Verse 4

> Nevertheless, I have this against you, that you have left your first love.

¶ **I have [this] against you**) This phrase creates an exception three times for those who possessed a failing alongside their good qualities. See also verses 14 and 20. It is a similar way of speaking to Matthew 5:23: *That your brother has something against you.* If one is expected to settle matters with a brother, how much more so with the Lord—and indeed, without delay.

¶ **Your first love**) He still possessed love; otherwise, so many laudable qualities would not have remained in him. However, he had not preserved that first, tender love amidst his great busyness and his zeal. Alongside zeal against the wicked, gentleness toward the good must remain. <note>The author suggests that in the heat of defending the faith, the Ephesian church had lost the softness and warmth of their initial devotion.</note>

2. That which is first or former serves as a pattern against which subsequent things should be measured, to see whether they have become diminished or more complete (see verse 5 and 19; also 1 Timothy 5:12).

3. Love in particular is of primary importance (verse 19). One should compare this with the entire Epistle of Paul to the Ephesians. <note>St. Paul's letter to the Ephesians emphasizes love and unity, making this later reproach in Revelation particularly poignant.</note>

---

### Verse 5

> Remember therefore from where you have fallen, and repent, and do the first works. Or else I will come to you and will remove your lampstand from its place, unless you repent.

¶ **Remember**) <note>The catchword "Ge-" from the original transcription likely refers to "Gedenke," the first word of this verse.</note> This is the first step toward recovery: recognizing the height of the spiritual state from which one has slipped. 

¶ **Repent**) <term>Repentance: from the German 'Busse,' implying a complete change of mind and heart, not merely a feeling of regret.</term> 

¶ **Remove your lampstand**) The lampstand represents the church's status and presence before God. To have it moved "from its place" is a warning of the loss of their light and their standing as a true congregation of Christ.

In these seven steps, the first and the second have the same tone: but there is this difference: that in the first step a period of time is given, alongside repentance, to also do the former works; in the second, however, only repentance is required. In the third step stands the word <term>I will be there</term> <note>original Greek: ἥξω (hēxō)</note>, which is also closer to <term>the future</term> <note>original Latin: in futuro</note> than <term>I come</term> <note>original Greek: ἔρχομαι (erchomai)</note>: and in the fourth, that former word is used twice, and indeed with sharper emphasis. In the fifth step, it is no longer called <term>I will be there</term>, and instead the word "quickly" is added, and in the sixth, the coming is very near. In the seventh step, it is indicated three times in succession, and with ever-increasing emphasis. Anyone will recognize the distinction, if not in all the steps, then at least in the beginning, middle, and end.

2. By the time the reader (see chapter I, verse 3) made his rounds through the seven churches, the Lord broke in with His preliminary coming; which was then a joyful representation and vision of the Last Day and Judgment for the good, and a terrifying one for the evil. The order of reading went somewhat slowly, perhaps week by week, from Ephesus to Laodicea, from West to East <note>original: "von Abend gegen Morgen" — literally "from evening toward morning," indicating the geographic direction of the seven churches in Asia Minor.</note>; but the coming happens quickly, like a flash of lightning, from East to West <note>original: "von Morgen gegen Abend."</note>.

# II. 10. Fear nothing — give.

<page-num>241</page-num>
<header>Fear nothing — give. II. 10.</header>
<sig>Q</sig>

...two had already passed. 3. It is not found that all these persecutions affected Smyrna specifically, or at least always before other places. 4. Those were ten separate tribulations, or at least several; however, here the text speaks of a single, ten-day, uninterrupted tribulation. 5. The ten days cannot be reconciled with the period of more than 200 years during which those persecutions occurred. The last of these persecutions, primarily under Diocletian <note>Emperor Diocletian (reigned 284–305 AD) led the "Great Persecution," the empire's last and most severe wave of Christian persecution.</note>, fits just as poorly here, even though it lasted for ten years. For 1. it is far too distant from the date of the prophecy, and 2. it did not affect the saints in Smyrna in such a particularly special and uninterrupted way. 3. All preceding persecutions would be skipped over. 4. A prophetic day is not an entire year. <note>The author refers to the "year-day principle," a method of interpretation where one day in a vision represents one literal year of history; he argues that here the days are literal.</note> Introduction § 38. 39. What then are these ten days? Here, at the beginning of the book, the language is not yet so veiled; and thus we understand it as literal, natural days, just as in verses 13 and 21, the words "days" and "period" are understood naturally. It must have been a sharp tribulation, perhaps a final portion of the persecution under Domitian <note>Emperor Domitian (reigned 81–96 AD); tradition holds he was the emperor who exiled the Apostle John to Patmos.</note>, until the edict of Emperor Nerva <note>Nerva (reigned 96–98 AD) succeeded Domitian and ended many of his predecessor's harsher policies, including the persecution of Christians.</note> to stop the persecution was followed even in Smyrna. Whether one understands these ten days as natural or prophetic days, the specific historical record is simply not available to us in our time.

### The 17th Verse.

> He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches: To the one who overcomes I will give some of the hidden manna; and I will give him a white stone, and on the stone a new name written, which no one knows except the one who receives it.

Another contrast, between two kinds of food, stands in Hebrews 13:9–10. The secret new name corresponds to this hidden manna. In the ancient **Ark of the Covenant**, the manna was kept as a memorial, Hebrews 9:3; and the heavenly Ark of the Covenant is seen in Revelation 11:19, under the trumpet of the seventh angel. At that time, the hidden manna will surely be brought forth: this is followed by freedom from the <term>second death</term> <note>A term in Revelation referring to eternal separation from God, rather than physical death.</note> during the thousand years: and the eating from the **tree of life** in the new Jerusalem.

¶ **A white stone)** or, a small white stone. The ancients expressed their <term>votes</term> <note>original: "Vota"</note> and opinions with stones on many occasions: and in those times, black stones were unfavorable <note>signifying condemnation or a "no" vote</note>, and white stones were favorable <note>signifying acquittal or a "yes" vote</note>. Sometimes they also wrote on stones or <term>potsherds</term> <note>Broken pieces of pottery used as cheap writing surfaces.</note>. Both of these ancient customs are aimed at here simultaneously.

## II. 24. To you however — another burden.

¶ (**To you — the rest**) A gracious distinction! <term>Father Simon<note>Richard Simon (1638–1712) was a prominent French priest and biblical critic known for his pioneering work in historical-critical linguistics of the Bible.</note></term> translates it neatly: *with regard to the rest of you* <note>original French: "à l'égard de vous autres"</note>.

2. Concerning the good people at **Sardis**, it says: **you have a few names**; it does not say, "there are few of you." ¶ (**This**) namely, Jezebel's teaching.

¶ (**Who have not known**) These good souls did not know it; they did not concern themselves with inquiring into such things, and thus remained unentangled by them. A secure and peaceful ignorance for those whom it does not concern!

See verse 9.

### The 25th Verse.

> Only what you have, hold fast, until I shall come.

### The 26th Verse.

> And whoever overcomes, and whoever keeps my works until the end, to him I will give power over the nations.

¶ **And**) With this little word, this specific one among the seven promises begins. From which it can be concluded that this assurance has a special connection with the preceding address. The following remark deals with this.

¶ **He who overcomes and he who keeps** etc.) These are two kinds of people with their respective duties. The **overcomer** has a struggle beforehand, and especially at the last <note>German: *auf die Letze*, referring to the final struggle of life or the end times.</note>, and thus receives a victory in death. Whoever does not have and maintain such a struggle and victory should nevertheless keep the works of Christ, namely until the end. **Overcoming** means maintaining loyalty and faith until death; the **keeping of the works** of Christ is patience and the doing of the commandments, even when an enemy is no longer present and there is nothing more to overcome. Chapter XXII. 14. Only in this fourth letter is this latter part added to the former. The Lord wishes to lay no other burden upon the rest in Thyatira; thus they also—which is a rare thing—did not have much further to fight, and besides overcoming, it is required of them that they **should keep the works of Christ until the end.**

¶ **The nations)** This book mentions the nations very often, and at this first instance I wish to explain why I use this word instead of "the heathens." A heathen (*Pagan* <note>original: *Paganus*, a Latin term for a villager or rustic, which the author interprets as someone banished from the city to the "heath" or countryside</note>) is an individual person: whereas a <term>nation <note>original Greek: ἔθνος (*ethnos*)</note></term> is a multitude even in the singular, and is sometimes even said of Israel. Luke VII. 5. But through "the nations" in the plural, something much greater is expressed.

<header>III. 2. Wake up — to my God.</header>

¶ **And the seven stars)** These seven stars have already been mentioned in chapter II, 1, just as the seven golden lampstands are subordinated to them, repeated from the first chapter. And because nothing else from Chapter I is repeated twice in Chapters II and III, this is an indication that the seven stars are mentioned here only incidentally, insofar as they are subordinated to the seven spirits of God. <note>The author suggests the "stars" (angels/leaders of churches) are under the direct influence and authority of the "seven spirits" (the fullness of the Holy Spirit).</note>

¶ **That you have a name)** In the Scriptures, a name that exists without the deed is often rejected or denied, as seen in Ruth 1:20 <note>In Ruth 1:20, Naomi says, "Do not call me Naomi [Pleasant]; call me Mara [Bitter]," because her circumstances did not match her name.</note> and Jeremiah 20:3. And the book of Revelation, in particular, suffers no false names, as seen in chapter II, verses 2 and 9. The name of the angel <note>In this context, "angel" refers to the pastor or leader of the congregation.</note> of the congregation at Sardis might have been derived from "life" in Greek or some other language—at least he stood in good credit—but in reality, the opposite was true of him, just as it was with the one at Laodicea, who held himself in such high regard. Everywhere the Lord Jesus looks to the foundation: before His eyes, all empty appearance, slander, and imagination must vanish. Ch. II, 2 etc.

> **Wake up, and strengthen what remains, which was about to die. For I have not found your works complete before my God.**

¶ **Wake up)** Precisely through this word of awakening, sleep is taken from him. Ephesians 5:14. <note>original: *Werde wachend*; literally "become waking." The author references the command to "Awake, O sleeper" to show that God's word carries the power to effect the change it commands.</note>

### III. 7. And to the — opens.

He proves Himself as the faithful and true One through His unchanging power to open and to close.

¶ **The key of David**) A master of a household or a prince possesses one or more keys with which he can open and shut the doors of his house or palace and all its rooms; in this same way, David also had a key, which was later granted to Eliakim <note>Eliakim was a high-ranking official under King Hezekiah. In Isaiah 22:22, he is given the "key of the house of David," signifying his absolute authority as the king's representative.</note>. See Isaiah 22:22. How much more, then, does Christ—the Son of David—possess the fortress-key <term>Burg-Schlüssel: a term denoting the primary key to a stronghold, symbolizing supreme administrative and royal power</term> of David and all royal authority in His house.

¶ **He who**) This phrase refers not to the key itself, but to the Lord Himself.

¶ **He who opens and no one shuts, and He shuts and no one opens**) O, what great power! Whatever He does remains settled and final. Compare Isaiah 22:22 and Job 12:14. Blessed is the person who stands under the protection of this Lord.

¶ **Opens**) This refers to the progress and advancement of His works and His servants.

¶ **No one**) Meaning no enemy; and also no well-intentioned person who might occasionally wish to take a different path than the one the Lord Himself has chosen.

¶ **Shuts**) This is done to keep out and hold back everything that is contrary or harmful.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Revelation 3:10, specifically concluding the discussion on the "world-circle" (the inhabited world) before moving on to distinguish between the terms "world-circle" and "earth," and identifying the historical context of the "hour of temptation" as the persecution under Emperor Trajan.</meta>

# III. 10. Because—upon the earth.
<meta>catchword: The</meta>

established. The same is also mentioned in chapters 12:9, 16:14, and 20:2.

¶ **World-circle— (Earth)** These two words mean the same thing, and yet the former sounds somewhat grander. The **world-circle** is named here in regard to the hour: and the **earth** in regard to the temptation itself. This hour passed over the Christians and over the Jews and Pagans, but with a great distinction for the true Christians: and it might have been related to the persecution under the seemingly virtuous Emperor Trajan. <note>Trajan (reigned 98–117 AD) was known as a "good" emperor, but his legal responses to Pliny the Younger established a formal procedure for prosecuting Christians who refused to worship Roman gods.</note> The two previous persecutions were not such great temptations, for they were organized by two openly wicked emperors, Nero and Domitian: but Trajan had the surname <term>the Best</term> <note>original: "Optimi", a title granted to Trajan by the Senate to denote him as the "best of rulers" (Optimus Princeps).</note> ruler, and his decree was of such a nature that only then was there a notable temptation for those who **dwelt upon the earth**. The pagans acquired an even greater dread of Christianity, the Jews poured oil on the fire, rejoiced, and stiffened their resolve, and the Christians were placed in either doubt or fear. The fourth persecution under <term>Antoninus the Philosopher</term> <note>Better known today as the Emperor Marcus Aurelius (reigned 161–180 AD).</note> occurred only about 60 years after the date of the Revelation, and particularly in France.

¶ **Those who dwell upon the earth)** These are generally natural and earthly-minded people.

### Verse 20.

> Behold, I have come to stand at the door and I knock: if anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and eat supper with him, and he with me.

¶ **At the door**) Thus the coming <term>Original: "Zukunft," referring here to the Second Coming or Advent of Christ.</term> of the Lord is very near. James 5:9. He lets His voice be heard at the door by speaking these very words.

¶ **Anyone**) Oh, how kindly Jesus invites Himself to us.
