# Conclusion of the Explanation of Chapters II and III.

With what we have reported, the purpose of these seven letters is, we hope, fulfilled. Many interpreters <term>Ausleger; scholars who provide formal explanations of biblical texts</term> strive to derive from these seven letters successive periods <note>original: "Periodos"</note> and eras <note>original: "Zeitläuffe"</note>, or rather states, of the universal Christian church. They have diligently embellished this opinion for a considerable time and made it common in the German language as well as in others. However, if the seven letters were intended to represent seven states of the church, why should the universal church not be divided into seven locations, climates, and regions rather than seven time periods? For the lampstand at Ephesus has its specific station or place (Chapter II:5), and consequently, so do the others; and the seven spirits of God, under which the seven stars stand (Chapter III:1), are sent out into all the earth. In every way, the seven letters concern the universal church in all places and at all times; yet one will find within them neither seven distinct locations nor seven distinct eras. The former is suspected by no one and therefore requires no refutation; and if the latter were to be the case, and we were to interweave the addresses to the seven angels of the congregations and to some of the congregations themselves, as well as the promises for those who overcome...

<meta>catchword: other [ander]</meta>

<summary>The author concludes the commentary on Revelation chapters 2 and 3 by arguing against the popular "church age" theory, suggesting that the seven letters apply to the entire church at all times rather than representing chronological eras.</summary>

# Conclusion of the Explanation.

...otherwise cast <note>original: "ander werfen"; this continues the sentence from the previous page suggesting a different arrangement of interpretation</note> them, we could also derive from the seven letters, and according to their sequence, seven successive states <term>Zustände; refers to specific conditions or eras of the church's history</term>. These would follow one another in a gradually and orderly increasing duration, using no more force than others apply.
The **I** would be the Period <note>original: "Periodus"</note> of the unmasked false apostles, at the end of the 1st and the beginning of the 2nd century.
The **II** would be that of the defeated false Jews, in the 2nd century.
The **III** would be that of raging paganism, in the 3rd century.
The **IV** would be that of confused Christianity, from the 4th until the 9th century.
The **V** would be that of dead faith, from the 9th century until the defeat of the enemies.
The **VI** would be that of the prevailing true power: in the impending fulfillment of the great promises.
The **VII** would be that of the final security, toward the end of the world.

These seven states could proceed alongside the trumpets of the seven angels, just as we interpret them. Therefore, no one should interpret it as a self-serving inclination toward other preconceived notions simply because I cannot force my eyes to perceive such seven states. I have other reasons:
1. The Old Testament has such prototypes <term>Fürbilder; prophetic models or "types" in the Old Testament that foreshadow New Testament events</term>: the New Testament does not.

<meta>This page continues the author’s systematic argument against interpreting the seven churches of Revelation as chronological "eras" or "states" of church history. # Of Chapters II and III.

**II.** All seven stars and seven lampstands are described as being present among "what is" <note>original: "unter dem, was ist"; a reference to Revelation 1:19, where John is told to write what he has seen, the things that are, and the things that will happen hereafter</note>. See Chapter 1:19–20. And after the prophecy has been attached in this same manner, Chapter 4:1 begins in an orderly fashion with that which is to happen hereafter.

**III.** The defenders of the seven church states <term>Kirchen-Zustände; the theological theory that the seven churches represent seven distinct chronological eras of the Christian church</term> unanimously begin their timeline from the lifetime of John. However, they are unable to set a definitive end point for these eras—especially for the seventh—and therefore cannot achieve a reliable division into seven distinct parts, particularly since no specific duration of time is expressed in the prophecy.

**IV.** Regarding the trumpets, the text says: the first, the second, the third angel sounded, *etc.* Indeed, later with the bowls <term>Schalen; often called the "vials of wrath" in older English translations</term>, the first and second angels are mentioned, and so on; and previously, the first and second seals <term>Sigel</term> were also noted. If the seven congregations and their angels were intended to represent seven successive states of the New Testament church, then it would be phrased just as it is with the trumpets—and even more so than with the seals and bowls—saying: "To the first angel of the first congregation write," *etc.*, speaking of all of them in this way until the seventh angel of the seventh congregation.

**V.** The lampstands and the stars—that is, the seven congregations and their angels—exist simultaneously. For Christ walks in the midst of the seven golden lampstands (Chapter 2:1, 3:1), and just as the seven spirits of God exist together, so too are the seven stars held together in His right hand.

### IV. 2. And immediately—one sat.

<margin>Introduction §§ 4, 5, 6</margin>In describing human actions, it is something noble and excellent when one sets forth not only the course of events, but also the occasion, the causes, the intentions, the means, the detours, the obstacles, the counter-arrangements, the outcome, and the success. Even more does this befit divine wisdom, both in history and in prophecy. In Isaiah, beautiful examples of this are found, and especially, as noted, this is found in the Revelation of Jesus Christ. Indeed, this book describes not only what occurs on earth in terms of good and evil, but also how things originate <note>original: *urständen*; a word often used in mystical German theology to describe the primal "rising" or "originating" of spiritual realities</note> in the realm of light and partly in the realm of darkness, and how they are drawn back there again.

3. Certainly, no one can derive these fourth and fifth chapters and many other such things from the form and history of the **Church Militant** <term>Church Militant: From the Latin *ecclesia militans*; the Christian church on earth which is still "fighting" against sin, the world, and the devil, in contrast to the Church Triumphant in heaven.</term>; and for this reason, one should not demand of any interpreter that he demonstrate it from there. Much less should one accuse him as if he were seeking an empty excuse for a lack of historical interpretation under the pretext of heavenly things. Otherwise, it would be an easy matter, for example, to derive the virtues of the Christian congregation and its leaders from the characteristics of the **four heavenly creatures** <note>original: *vier himmlische Thiere*; the "living creatures" described in Revelation 4:6–8, often associated with the four Gospels or various virtues</note>.

4. Regarding the **throne**, it is properly said not that it *stood*, but that it *lay* <note>The author is likely referencing the specific Greek word used in Revelation 4:2, *ekeito*, which suggests being "set" or "placed" in a way that implies stability or breadth</note>. By which its very great breadth is indicated.

### Verse 3.

> And he who sat there was to look upon like a jasper and a sardius stone, and a rainbow was all around the throne, in appearance like an emerald.

White signifies purity; **Red** signifies zeal against evil; **Green** signifies grace toward the children of the covenant. This lovely color also makes the white and the red bearable to us.

This formed the boundary, so that those who were around the throne might come near enough to it, and yet not too near.

### Verse 4.

> And round about the throne were twenty-four thrones, and upon the thrones sat twenty-four elders, clothed in white garments, and on their heads were golden crowns.

¶ **Sitting)** They sit when they give their assent to the divine judgments; they fall down when they worship the LORD (Verse 10; Chapter 5:14; Chapter 11:16).

### IV, 6. And before the — and behind.

¶ **Like a sea of glass)** A **sea** is a large collection of many **waters**, and this word carries that same meaning here, whereby one has no reason to think of a large stand or vessel, such as was in Solomon’s temple <note>original: *Tempel Salomonis*; the author distinguishes this vision from the "Molten Sea," the large bronze basin used by priests for ritual washing in the Old Testament (1 Kings 7:23).</note>. What John saw here was a **sea**, wide and deep: like **glass**, in that the water was transparent and stood still: **like unto crystal**, entirely white, clear, and pure.

2. **What is this sea?** The seven **lamps of fire and the sea** are mentioned together: and it is said of this, just as with those, very emphatically: **before the throne.** Thus, this [the sea] along with those [the lamps] may point to the seven Spirits of God, just as in Chapter 5:6 both the seven horns and the seven eyes of the Lamb are interpreted as the seven Spirits of God, which are sent forth into all the earth. For the powers and workings of the Holy Spirit are very often presented under the images of fire and water. Later, in Chapter 15:2, there is again something **like a sea of glass**, and there the seven lamps of fire are not mentioned, but instead the sea itself is mingled with fire. Finally, in Chapter 22:1, there is a **river of the water of life**, clear as crystal: therefore the sea that is before the throne, and the river that proceeds from the throne of God and of the Lamb, may have the same interpretation, referring to the Spirit of God. 5. **Holy** means in Hebrew, Greek, Latin, German, etc., <note>The author refers to the terms *qādôš*, *hagios*, and *sanctus* discussed on the previous page.</note> as much as "separated": and when God is called holy, it indicates His quite special, unique excellence, and the radiance flowing together from His divine attributes, shining forth from all His works, and darkening everything outside of Himself; for He is and remains distinguished and removed in an incomparable and incomprehensible manner, not only from everything that is impure, but also from all that is merely of a creaturely nature.

6. God is **separated** from everything: He is and works from Himself, out of Himself, in Himself, through Himself, before Himself, and for His own sake. Therefore He is the first and the last, the unique and eternal, living and blessed, infinite and unchangeable, almighty, omniscient, wise and true, righteous and faithful, gracious and merciful.

7. Hence it follows that "Holy" and "Holiness" mean just as much as "God" and "Godhead": and just as one says of a king, "His Majesty," so the Scripture says of God, "His Holiness." Hebrews 12:10. The Holy Spirit is the Spirit of God. "The Holy One" is often used as a name when God is being spoken of.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Revelation Chapter 5, Verse 1. ### Verse 1: And I — seven seals. [319]

...to interpret. In the first, fifth, and seventh seals, no judgment breaks out at all; and the "third woe" <note>The Book of Revelation describes three "woes" associated with the final three trumpet blasts, signifying intense periods of distress.</note> belongs only to the trumpet of the seventh angel. Under that same woe, the beast and the harlot <note>In apocalyptic literature, these figures represent corrupt political and religious systems set against the divine order.</note> appear with their raging and eventual downfall. The opinion that limits the seven seals—as well as the seven trumpets and the seven bowls—solely to the aforementioned judgment causes many important matters in the prophecy to fall away. It loses the connection <note>original: "Connexion"</note> between future events already foretold in the Old and New Testaments <note>original: "A. und N. T." for Altes und Neues Testament</note>. Such a view cannot hold up against the wondrous order of this book. On the other hand, we find everything that this other opinion seeks in the seven seals and other places, gathered instead in abundance in Chapters 16, 18, and 19. Beyond these, from this point forward, we have many other things as well, appearing in their natural order.

The book and its seven seals demonstrate the power of Christ over all visible and invisible creatures. (See Introduction § 14 ff., 20 ff., 55). The copy of the book is contained within these chapters of Revelation. It was, so to speak, a sealed sevenfold order <term>order: original "Ordre," referring to an official decree or a set of instructions to be executed</term> of very rich and manifold content. This content is appropriate to the majesty of the scene opened in the fourth chapter and the solemnity of everything that is now further seen and heard in the fifth chapter.

<summary>This page argues that the seven seals represent a broad scope of Christ's authority over all creation rather than just the final judgment. The author critiques interpretations that compress all prophetic events into the final judgments, emphasizing the "natural order" and continuity of biblical prophecy.</summary>

### Verse 2.

> And I saw a mighty angel, who called out with a loud voice: Who is worthy to open the book and to break its seals?

¶ **A mighty angel)** This proclamation to all of creation would be too high a task for a human, and not fitting for the Little Lamb <note>original: "Lämmlein." ¶ **To open)** For this very purpose, the book was publicly displayed by the one who sat upon the throne.

# V. 6. And I saw — the whole earth.

Jesus Christ was killed in the 33rd year of His life on earth; therefore He is rightly called a **little Lamb** <note>original: "Lämmlein," a diminutive emphasizing His youth and innocence compared to the long lives of the patriarchs.</note>; the ancient patriarchs lived 20 to 30 times as long.

Precisely because the little Lamb allowed Himself to be slaughtered, He is worthy to open the book, verse 9; Philippians 2:8–9. This is for the delight of His own (verse 9) and for the terror of His enemies (chapter 6:16).

Likewise, in Zechariah 3:9, and even more explicitly in chapter 4:10, the seven eyes of the Lord, which go throughout the whole earth, are praised.

8. However, the actions of each rider do indeed go *to specific details* <note>original: "ad specialia"</note> and provide a pattern of how, very soon after the date of this prophecy, the following will occur:

I. toward the **East** <note>original: "gegen Morgen"; literally "toward the morning," the traditional German term for the East.</note>: dominion, and victory upon victory, far and wide;
II. toward the **West** <note>original: "gegen Abend"; literally "toward the evening," the traditional German term for the West.</note>: much bloodshed;
III. toward the **South** <note>original: "gegen Mittag"; literally "toward midday," the traditional German term for the South.</note>: scarcity of produce <note>Referring to famine or high prices for grain.</note>;
IV. toward the **North** <note>original: "gegen Mitternacht"; literally "toward midnight," the traditional German term for the North.</note>: plague and various calamities in extraordinary measure.

9. An image of victory is found in the first seal: the rider on the white horse, who carries a bow. The bow drives arrows into the distance, and the white color of the horse signifies prosperity, expanded borders, the overcoming of many peoples, and triumph.

10. A very different, quite special, and incomparable rider on a white horse appears in Chapter 19:11 <note>This later figure is widely interpreted by theologians as Jesus Christ returning in glory.</note>; but this one in the first seal must be understood in proportion with the riders of the second, third, and fourth...

11. I do not dare to say that each rider in the first four seals is a powerful spirit. Their meaning is provided by what is visible: and even if by "Death" in the fourth seal a personal **Angel of Death**, as an individual, were to be understood (as a new interpretation claims without proof), it still could not be concluded from this that the riders in the first three seals are also specific persons. 12. At the very time when the Revelation <note>The Book of Revelation or the Apocalypse of John.</note> was being written, Nerva succeeded Emperor Domitian, in the year 96 <note>original: "A 96"; Anno 96.</note>, on September 18th. He ruled alone for barely a year, and his only major act of state was that, three months before his death, he named Trajan as his son, co-regent, and successor. Trajan received news of this in Cologne on the Rhine and set out for Rome; Nerva, however, died in the year 98, on January 27th. The reign of this Emperor Trajan is of such uniquely great importance that one cannot skip over it when considering the fulfillment of what was "soon to happen" <note>A reference to the opening of Revelation, which speaks of events that must shortly take place.</note>; rather, his entry into Rome should rightly be considered the dawn of the Seven Seals.

¶ **And he went out, conquering and to conquer**) namely, with victory, toward victory. In the year 108, the already victorious **Trajan** marched out toward the East <note>original: "gegen Morgen," literally "toward the morning," an archaic German term for the East</note> so that he might conquer the peoples in **Armenia, Assyria, Mesopotamia,** etc., even beyond the **Tigris**, so that the borders of the **Roman Empire**, which had previously been so greatly expanded on that side by **Pompey**, fell far within **Trajan’s** territory. One finds no other emperor like him in victorious expeditions or in making **conquests** <note>original: "Conquêten"</note>, whereas his successor **Hadrian** <note>original: "Adrianus"</note> voluntarily gave up the aforementioned three provinces beyond the **Euphrates**. This also serves to explain the phrase where it says *that he conquered*. What did **Trajan** and the empire gain from it? Nothing else but that he simply conquered. This is the life of such conquerors. Meanwhile, through **Trajan**, that which was prophesied of the **fourth empire** in **Daniel 2:40** and **7:23** was particularly fulfilled: that it would *devour, trample, and crush all lands.*

### VI. 6. And I — no harm.

Out of a bushel <note>original: "Scheffel"; a historical dry measure</note> one makes about 112 pounds of bread: and thus from a quart <note>original: "Vierling"</note> or *choenix* <note>original: "Chœnix"; a Greek measure roughly equal to a liter</note> three and a half pounds <note>original: "vierthalb Pfund"</note>. That would be expensive enough for 10 kreuzers <note>original: "Kreuzer"; a small silver coin common in the author's time</note>.

¶ **And three quarts of barley for a ten-piece** ) Either barley was generally much cheaper among the ancients than wheat: or the prophecy states it here as something special beforehand, that barley will be three times as cheap as wheat. One pound of wheat bread for three kreuzers: three pounds of barley bread for three kreuzers.

¶ **And to the oil and the wine do no harm** ) Thus the rider would have caused damage to the oil and wine, had it not been forbidden to him. Barley and wheat ripen earlier than oil and wine. Here the text speaks of a time that is better for oil and wine than for barley and wheat. This taken together points to a moderate scarcity <note>original: "Theurung"; refers to a time of high prices or famine</note>; especially since one can compensate for the lack of one kind of food with the supply of the other. Wheat and barley, oil and wine, are the most common and necessary provisions. Thus the command given here to the rider carries a great deal of weight.

### VI. 8. And I looked — of the earth.

*And what pestilence, famines, and fires occurred. In all of these, Trajan provided much help through excellent remedies... Therefore, he was deservedly called the Father of his Country.* <note>original Latin: "QUE PESTILENTIA, FAMESQUE, & incendia facta sunt. Quibus omnibus Trajanus per exquisita remedia plurimum opitulatus est...... Vnde merito pater patriæ dictus est." This quote highlights the Roman Emperor Trajan's reputation for disaster relief, which the author uses to date the fulfillment of this prophecy.</note> The **dying** <note>original: "Sterben"; in early modern German, this word specifically referred to the plague or a mass mortality event</note> actually signifies the **plague**, and yet one can also understand under this **earthquakes**, **fire**, and **distress of water** <note>referring to floods or maritime disasters</note>, insofar as many people are killed by them with violence. Not only the heathens but also the Jews threw many people to the beasts in those times: and it may well be that at that time, power was also otherwise given to the animals over mankind.

2. History does not provide us with as much detail as we ourselves might wish: yet this takes nothing away from the true interpretation for fair-minded souls. When an astronomer <note>original: "Sternseher"; literally "star-seer," referring here to a scientist who calculates celestial movements</note> correctly describes solar and lunar eclipses in advance, the visible eclipses serve even the inexperienced as proof that he has hit upon the others no less accurately, even if they were not seen in our own or other parts of the world. So it is also with prophecy <note>original: "Weissagung"</note> and its explanation. The parts whose undeniable success one sees in history provide proof that the other parts—of which there is a trace in the text indicating they cannot be explained at all from human history, or that they cannot be fully documented from the history known at the time—were nonetheless also accurately hit upon.

<vocab>Pestilence, Hunger, Trajan, Earthquake, Prophecy, History, Eclipses</vocab>

<summary>The author identifies the "dying" of the Fourth Seal with the plague and other natural disasters during the reign of Emperor Trajan. He argues that the partial historical evidence of fulfilled prophecy serves as proof for the accuracy of the entire prophetic vision, much like a predicted eclipse validates an astronomer's calculations.</summary>

3. Thus, what occurred during the times of Trajan served as a fourfold proof. It showed that the four horsemen remain subject to Christ at all times—according to His will, under His patience, and eventually for His vengeance against the wicked and for the service of the righteous. This applies not only to the specific outbreaks of that era, which (as mentioned) do not by any means exhaust the meaning of the first four seals, but also to all future events, whether similar or different. Consequently, the entire course of visible nature and the world—which is indeed a very great and significant thing—is under His authority. In this way, the path was prepared for the trumpets that follow immediately one after another; and through the prompt fulfillment of the first four seals, a credible reputation was established for the entire prophecy regarding the future.

4. In this manner, we must not restrict the explanation of the seals to mere specifics <note>original Latin: "Specialia"; referring to unique historical events</note>, as the defenders of the seven periods <note>original Latin: "Periodorum"; a method of interpreting Revelation as a chronological map of seven distinct eras of church history</note> are accustomed to doing; nor should we remain with pure generalities <note>original Latin: "Generalibus"</note>, as Marckius <note>Johannes Marckius (1656–1731), a Dutch theologian known for his systematic approach to prophecy</note> among the moderns has done, believing he could refute the former more effectively by doing so.

### VI. 9. And when he — had held.

¶ **And)** The three latter seals have a unique connection with one another: for they encompass the invisible realm within themselves. They do so in such a way that in the fifth seal, the blessed departed—especially the martyrs as the most prominent—come into view; in the sixth, the inhabitants of the underworld <note>original Latin: "Inferi"; referring to the unblessed deceased or those in the lower realms</note> or the unblessed deceased; and in the seventh, the holy angels with their attendance and service during the great events that will occur through the seven trumpets, as well as the dragon and his angels appearing under the trumpet of the seventh angel. Those who strive to derive the entire prophecy solely from church and world histories, while excluding or ignoring the realms of heaven and hell, do not only exhaust themselves in vain, but they also possess far too shallow a concept of the incomparable majesty of this prophecy.

¶ **I saw)** Since John was able to see the angels, he was also able to see the souls.

¶ **Under the altar)** John speaks of secret things—even when he mentions them for the first time—often as if they were things already known to the listener (or at least to himself) from other testimonies of divine truth or from the present vision, or things that are now meant to become known through him. Thus, he does not say here *under an altar*, but rather, **under the altar**. One may compare his expression regarding the seven angels who stand before <meta>catchword: God</meta>

They are concerned with the glory of their Lord’s holiness and truth: and this glory resounds in chapter XIX. 2, where the martyrs’ desire is transposed into a song of praise with a most remarkable repetition of their words. ### VI. 11. And it was — they too.

The angel swears in Chapter 10:6-7 that from the moment of his oath until the completion of the mystery of God, there will be no more <term>Time</term> <note>original: "Chronon." The author interprets the Greek word *chronos* as a technical unit of 1,111.11 years.</note> remaining. This <term>No-More-Time</term> <note>original: "Non-chronus"</note> presupposes a period of "Time," and one could not know what the "No-More-Time" is if a "Time"—and specifically an absolute "Time" so named—were not found in the prophecy. However, this is to be found nowhere else but here in the fifth seal. Therefore, one must read here not "a little time," but simply "a time" <note>original: "einen Chronon"</note>, before the end of which that "No-More-Time"—which is the opposite of this "Time"—enters. Thus, both together fill the entire space from <term>John’s lifetime</term> <note>Referring to the Apostle John, the traditional author of Revelation.</note> until the completion of the mystery of God. For my part, I can make sense of my system even if one lets the little word "little" stand; but one cannot build anything, let alone so much, upon this at least uncertain little word from the very start. And even if it were correct, it would not follow that this "little interval" here and the "short time" or "three and a half times" <note>original: "vierthalb Zeit." An archaic German expression meaning three and a half (the fourth unit is only a half).</note> in Chapter 12:12, 14 are the same thing, just as the "little interval" in Chapter 20:3 is not the same as these periods of time.

# And it was — they too. [Revelation] VI. 11.

The <term>No-More-Time</term> <note>original: "Non-chronus." Refers to Revelation 10:6, often translated as "there should be time no longer."</note> would be testified and so solemnly sworn only much later; rather, it simply says that these souls should go to **rest** for one more <term>Time</term> <note>original: "Chronon." Abraham was shown how long it would last from his time until the departure from the <term>house of bondage</term> <note>Referring to the Israelites' slavery in Egypt.</note>; but afterward, 40 years in the wilderness were added (Genesis XV. 13, 16). And so here too, between the crying out of the souls and the completion of their fellow servants and brothers, a "Time" <note>original: "Chronus"</note> is set, after the end of which some space still remains. Yet this "Time" reaches significantly into the times of the Beast—during which there is new bloodshed—until the judgment and vengeance occur even before the Beast’s downfall.

### VII, 1. And—any tree.

¶ **Upon the four corners of the earth**) East, West, South, and North. <note>The author uses the archaic German terms "Morgen" (Morning), "Abend" (Evening), "Mittag" (Midday), and "Mitternacht" (Midnight) to denote the four cardinal directions based on the sun's position.</note> Intro. § 21. The trumpets of the first four angels proceed in this order: and at all four ends of the world, there are servants of God from Israel. Isaiah 43:5, 6; 49:12.

¶ **Who held the four winds, that no wind might blow**) In nature, winds—provided they do not come too violently—are something very useful, pleasant, and indispensable. Now, the trumpets of the first, second, and third angels carry much fire with them, Chapter 8:7ff, whose hot, harmful, and bitter effects might have been cooled, dispersed, and mitigated by the winds. But because the four angels hold the four winds (which is a task of quite long duration), they damage the earth, the sea, and the trees by that very act. For the plagues under the aforementioned trumpets thereby maintain their unhindered progress.

¶ **On the earth, nor on the sea, nor on any tree**) Let one look upon a general map of the world: for which part of the world is the designation "the Earth" most fitting? For that which lies toward the East <note>original: "gegen Morgen"; literally "toward the morning," referring to the Orient or the Levant.</note>, and is therefore the first. This part was the first to be inhabited by humans; the other parts are more closely connected to it than they are to one another. John on Patmos had this part closest to him, and it was there that the trumpet of the first angel found its fulfillment.

The author identifies "the Earth" specifically with the East (the Middle East/Levant) as the primary theater of these events.</summary>

# VII. 2. And I saw — the sea.

Thus the **earth** is Asia. In contrast, **Europe** swims in the **sea**, and for this reason is understood in the Prophets through the **islands**. The third remaining part, namely **Africa**, is indicated by the **streams of water**, or by the **trees** that grow frequently along the water-streams and soothe the heat with their great shade. Chapter 8:7, 8, 10. This is the actual reason why the sea stands here between the earth and the trees, whereas otherwise the trees would belong to the earth. Genesis 1:11. <note>The author is explaining why Revelation 7:1 lists "earth, sea, and trees" as three distinct categories. In the creation story of Genesis, trees are part of the earth, but here they represent a specific geographic region—Africa—distinguished by its river-fed vegetation.</note>

2. **The earth, the sea, the trees**, in this way constitute only three parts: where is the fourth region of the world? Answer: The trumpet of the fourth angel aims at the fourth region of the world, namely the North <note>original: "Mitternacht"; literally "midnight," a traditional German term for the North because the sun is at its lowest point there at that time.</note>; and within those three parts, the North might also be included, or perhaps under the trumpet of the fourth angel there was no such damage against which a sealing would be necessary for any Israelites.

### VII. 3. And spoke — their foreheads

# And I — Sons of Israel. VII. 4.

¶ **On their foreheads)** The seal is seen most clearly on the forehead. On their foreheads, the name of the Lamb and the name of His Father are also written later on Mount Zion. Chapter 14:1.

### The 4th Verse

**And I heard the number of those who were sealed, one hundred forty-four thousand sealed out of all the tribes of the sons of Israel.**

### VII. 3. And he said—their foreheads.

Chapter 14:1.

¶ **Nor the trees)** Africa is indicated in Chapter 8:10 by the rivers; but here, it is indicated by the trees. For the holding back of the four winds is more fittingly applied to trees than to rivers. Chapter 7:1. <note>The author uses geographical allegory, common in historical-prophetic interpretations of this period, to link symbolic natural features with specific continents.</note>

¶ **Until)** Thus, the harm is otherwise permitted to those four angels <note>That is, the four angels who hold the winds are only restrained until the sealing is complete.</note>.

¶ **We)** The angel who rose from the sunrise <note>The East.</note> is not the only one who seals. He says: *until we seal*: and therefore he has helpers. ¶ **The servants of our God)** This noble title belongs especially to the saints out of Israel. Genesis 50:17 <note>original: "1 Mos. L. 17"; the first book of Moses.</note>; Isaiah 61:6.

<header>VII. 5-8. From the — sealed.</header>

None of these eight orders is random or without cause in its description, although the reasons may be clearer and more significant in one place than in another.

### II. These orders differ in many ways, yet they also agree in many ways.

Sometimes Ephraim and Manasseh are placed, sometimes again Levi and Joseph. Sometimes the number twelve remains constant, while at other times there is some change. Sometimes these tribes are joined together, and sometimes those, and they are arranged according to various regions of the world. However, much attention is paid to the order of birth (Exodus <note>Original: *2 Mos.* (Second Book of Moses)</note> XXVIII. 10), and the sons of the concubines <note>Original: *Kebsweiber*; referring to Bilhah and Zilpah, the handmaids of Rachel and Leah</note> must yield more and allow themselves to be positioned as is deemed fitting.

### III. Most often, the biological brothers from the same mother are placed pair by pair.

Leah bore six sons, Bilhah two, Zilpah two, and Rachel two: and therefore biological brothers are very often, and indeed several times, placed two and two together. Where they are placed three and three, the third is joined to the pair in a convenient manner.

6. Thus, in both **Ezekiel** and the Revelation, three tribes are arranged within this pair using a concise and instructive method. **Manasseh** was formerly the weakest tribe in terms of numbers (**Numbers 1:35**). However, because his father **Joseph** received the birthright (**1 Chronicles 5:1–2**) and thus received two portions of the inheritance, in **Ezekiel’s** [vision of the] great descendants, he also has two gates for entry into the city: one for **Ephraim**, under his own name **Joseph**, and additionally another for **Manasseh**. And so **Manasseh** now shares his gate with **Dan**, by virtue of the equal division of the tribes. **Dan**, with its small population, does not have a whole gate; yet for **Joseph** and **Manasseh**, a single gate is too little. One might therefore consider that the three tribes share two gates between them: **Joseph** and **Manasseh** having one and a half gates, and **Dan** having half a gate. Otherwise, no reason could be given why **Dan** is separated from the other sons of the concubines <note>Original: *Kebsweiber*; here referring to the handmaids Bilhah and Zilpah</note> and stands between the sons of **Leah** and **Rachel**. In this manner, the six sons of **Leah** occupy the sides of the North <note>Original: *Mitternacht* (Midnight)</note> and South <note>Original: *Mittag* (Midday)</note>; the sons of **Rachel** occupy the side of the East <note>Original: *Morgen* (Morning)</note>, and among **Joseph**, **Benjamin**, and **Dan**, the tribes of **Ephraim**, **Benjamin**, and **Manasseh** (**Psalm 80:2** <note>The original cites Psalm 80:3 following the numbering in the Luther Bible</note>) are indeed included. The remaining sons of the concubines close the side of the West <note>Original: *Abend* (Evening)</note>.

### From the — sealed ones. VII. 5-8.

7. Furthermore, in the Revelation, Dan is indeed not explicitly mentioned by name because of his insignificance <note>Original: *Wenigkeit*—referring to the small population or low status of the tribe at that time</note>. For this tribe, which after Judah was once the strongest (**Numbers 1:39, 2:31**), became very diminished due to its particular sluggishness in occupying its allotted land and its early fall into idolatry and captivity (**Judges 18:1, 30**); this is why the tribe is also passed over in **1 Chronicles 5 and 7**. According to the accounts of the ancient Hebrews, the tribe dwindled until only the family of **Hushim** remained. Because it did not come close to numbering 12,000, it is "tucked under" **Manasseh**. **Simeon** also became a minor and scattered tribe; therefore, he is placed (in the sixth order) under **Judah** (**Joshua 19:1, 9**), though in such a way that the word <term>Shama</term> <note>Hebrew: "to hear," the etymological root of the name Simeon</note>, from which the name **Simeon** is derived (**Genesis 29:33**), is echoed within the blessing of **Judah** in **Deuteronomy 33:7**. Similarly, Dan also has a portion here in the sealing. For it clearly states, **out of every tribe** (verse 4). If it had said, **out of the twelve tribes**, as in **Chapter 21:12**, one might think that Dan was excluded by the inclusion of **Levi** and **Manasseh**; but under the phrase "every tribe," Dan must also be present. And so he is found among the biological brothers placed <term>pair by pair</term> <note>Original: *par und par*</note> in the third pair. He is subsumed under **Manasseh**, and thus joined through **Manasseh** to his biological brother **Naphtali**; otherwise, **Manasseh** would not be positioned so far away from **Joseph** and **Benjamin** in the Revelation.

8. <header>After this — hands. VII. 9.</header>

Afterward, more such **hosts** <note>German: *Schaaren*—referring to companies or groups of people</note> appear, and with them always a higher or new level of **glory**, which they enter after a difficult struggle and a magnificent **victory**. (Chapter XIV. 1, XV. 2, XIX. 1, XX. 4). Each host explicitly praises that which they have experienced: and this first one praises the **rescue** or **salvation**. There is an unspeakable variety of levels of **reward** in that world. Let no one think: *If I just get into heaven, I will be satisfied.* Such a person might end up despising and missing heaven altogether. In worldly matters, people allow themselves to be moved by **ambition**, so that everyone pushes their "luck," as they call it, as high as they can. A far nobler **ambition** <note>2 Corinthians 5:9; Original Greek: *philotimia* (φιλοτιμια), meaning a striving or "love of honor" directed toward pleasing God</note> is appropriate for **believers**. The difference between the most excellent and the lowliest person in this world is nothing compared to even the smallest difference between the levels of glory in that world. Who has the time to consider this? Who conducts themselves accordingly?

¶ (**Which no one could number**) What a multitude that must be! While there are otherwise such large numbers in this book (v. 4, Chapter V. 11, IX. 16), this host is nevertheless uncountable.

¶ (**From every nation and tribe and people and language**) The **tribes** specifically refer to the people of **Israel**; otherwise, however, this fourfold naming encompasses the entire human— <note>The text continues on the next page: "human race."</note>

## The 15th Verse.

> Therefore they are before the throne of God, and serve Him day and night in His temple; and He who sits on the throne will spread His tabernacle over them.

¶ **Therefore)** because they are worthily equipped through the blood of the Lamb.

¶ **Throne — Throne)** Here it is reported concerning these blessed ones: 1. how they serve God, 2. what God shows toward them.

¶ **And serve Him)** <note>original: "warten ihm auf"; literally "to wait upon" or attend to someone, emphasizing service.</note> They thus come very close to the priestly dignity of the elders: yet there is a distinction. Here there are white stoles or robes; but not the [specific] white garments and golden crowns that the elders possess.

¶ **Day and night)** These blessed attendants may well have their orders and rotations <note>The author suggests a organized system of service, similar to the "courses" of priests in the Old Testament temple.</note>: for in between these times, they are led to the fountains of the water of life.

¶ **In His temple)** This temple is in heaven, and in heaven is the Ark of the Covenant: the angels go in and out there, and the holy commands proceed from that place. See, for example, chapters 11:19, 14:15, 14:17, 15:5, 15:8, 16:1, and 16:17.

¶ **Spread His tabernacle over them)** <note>original: "Seine Hütte über ihnen haben"; the German "Hütte" refers to a booth, tent, or the biblical Tabernacle.</note> By the very fact that they are in God’s temple, God’s dwelling is spread out over them, and the temple of the tabernacle of testimony (Chapter 15:5) acts as a protective shield over them. One should consider the passages concerning this heavenly tabernacle-dwelling in chapters 12:12, 13:6, and 21:3.

## Chapter Eight.

### Verse 1.

And when he opened the seventh seal, there was a silence in heaven for about half an hour. 2. And I saw the seven angels who stand before **God**, and seven trumpets were given to them.

¶ (**The seventh**) This is the most important of all the seals.

¶ (**A silence in heaven**) This silence is mentioned only in this single place, and is therefore something unusual and very significant <note>original: "bedenkliches"; in this 18th-century context, the term implies something that demands deep reflection or carries great weight, rather than something "dubious."</note>. Otherwise, the heavens are always sounding with praise, day and night (see Chapter 4:8; 5:10, 12). Most notably, just before this silence, all the angels—and before them the innumerable host of the saved <note>original: "Geretteten"; referring to those rescued or delivered from the Great Tribulation mentioned in the previous chapter.</note>—had let themselves be heard with a great voice (Chapter 7:10, 12). Now, all at once, it becomes still: everything pauses. During this silence, everything was also at rest, without movement or activity, until the seven trumpets were given to the seven angels. This also serves to markedly distinguish the seventh seal from the previous six. This pausing and silence before **God** indicates, among those who surround Him, a waiting accompanied by deep reverence for what great things the Divine Majesty will further reveal and ordain. Thus, the seven angels with their trumpets then...

# VIII. 3. And a — throne is.

One should look at what we noted regarding the previously cited passages in chapter 10:1 etc.; for now, we shall remain only with the present passage, as many evangelical teachers (see *Gnomon, p. 1116*) <note>The "Gnomon Novi Testamenti" is a famous 1742 commentary by Johann Albrecht Bengel, a central figure in Lutheran Pietism.</note> rightly understand this to be a created angel. For the angel with the golden censer is called **another** angel, so that he may be distinguished from the seven angels—not in terms of their nature as created beings, but in terms of their different task regarding the trumpets. Such an expression of **another** angel always signifies a likewise created angel. See chapters 7:2; 14:6, 8, 9, 15, 17, 18, etc.

Likewise, the act of **standing** by the **altar** (compared with Hebrews 10:11-12, where **standing** <note>original Greek: *hestēken*</note> is widely distinguished from **sitting** <note>original Greek: *ekathisen*; in Hebrews, the priest stands to serve, while Christ sits as Lord</note>), the receiving of the **incense**, and the angel's entire performance therein, is obviously a **ministerial** act <note>original: *dienstbares*, implying the role of a servant or subordinate</note>; therefore it is associated with the prayer of all the saints.

In summary, the word **angel** in the Revelation always refers to those actually called **angels**—at times **evil** ones, but commonly **good** ones—except for chapter 14:6, 8, 9. In that passage, since it speaks of **humans** <note>In the Protestant tradition of this era, the "three angels" of Revelation 14 were often interpreted as human reformers like Martin Luther.</note>, we shall note the specific reason for this exception.

To be sure, some wish to understand the "evangelical preaching office" <term>evangelische Predig-Amt: the institutional role of Protestant ministers and teachers</term> in this passage (chapter 8:3); however, here the service of the angel is directed toward GOD, whereas the name "angel" belongs to teachers and preachers only when they [deliver] a teaching from GOD’s behalf...

# VIII. 3. And a — throne is.

...saints, the angelic <note>original: *englische*; in this context, it refers to the actions of an angel rather than the English nation</note> incense-burning occurs. Both specifically refer to the future of the Kingdom of God. The angels are *fellow servants* of the saints, but not their *mediators*. When the divine decrees <note>original: *Rathschlüsse*; refers to God's predetermined plans or counsels</note> have been carried out, they praise God (Rev. 16:5); and when the time comes for them to be carried out, they long for it (Rev. 14:15, 18). And such is the longing of every creature according to its measure (Romans 8:22). In the times of the first persecutions, Christians prayed with great power and constant persistence. We noted regarding Chapter 5:8, however, that under the designation "saints," both the saints on earth and those in heaven are indicated: and since it explicitly says here, "of all saints," we understand both groups together; nevertheless, the invocation of departed saints for their intercession <note>original: *Fürbitte*</note>—as *Marckius in Ap. [Commentary on the Apocalypse] p. 203, 204* recognizes—finds no confirmation here. <note>The author is arguing against the Catholic practice of praying to saints, noting that while the angel handles the prayers of all saints, it does not mean humans should pray to deceased saints to act as go-betweens.</note> 

The small word "all" must not be restricted without urgent cause, especially in this book which encompasses so much (cf. Chapter 5:13, "all"), and in this passage, where that which is to be prayed for concerns the saints both on earth and in heaven. The two passages, Chapter 5:8 and Chapter 8:3–4, are closely connected: for there is very little space between the worship <note>original: *Anbetung*</note> which the four living creatures and the 24 elders offer to the Lamb <note>original: *Lämmlein*</note> and the incense-burning of the angel.

# And it rose up — before GOD. VIII. 4.

¶ **Upon the golden altar**, which is before the throne) It does not say "which is before the curtain <note>original: *Vorhang*; referring to the veil in the Tabernacle that separated the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place</note>." In the Temple at Jerusalem, the curtain was torn; but here, the discourse concerns a different, heavenly Temple.

### The 4th Verse.

**And the smoke of the incense rose up with the prayers of the saints from the hand of the angel before God.**

¶ **The smoke**) Such smoke was very pleasant. The words would actually be ordered like this: **The smoke of the incense rose up from the hand of the angel before God, together with the prayers of the saints.** But these very words are elegantly intertwined in the text to express correctly how the smoke and the prayers rose up at the same time. Both are together; both are heard.

¶ **From the hand**) It does not say that the prayers of the saints rose up *through* the hand of the angel. The angelic <note>original: *englische*; here meaning "of an angel," not the English language</note> incense does not need to be made pleasant by the prayers of the saints, and just as little do the prayers of the saints need to be made pleasant by the angelic incense. The angel did not have the censer <note>original: *Räuchpfanne*; a vessel for burning incense</note> in his hand during the burning of the incense; for afterwards it says that he took the censer, namely, after he had placed the incense upon the golden altar.

# VIII. 5. And the — Earthquake.

->The 5th Verse.<-

¶ **From the fire of the altar**) for vengeance upon the wicked world.

¶ **Thunders and lightnings and voices**) Here the thunders are listed first. In a powerful storm, one sometimes hears only the thunder, sometimes sees only the lightning, and sometimes everything happens all at once.

->The 6th Verse.<-

**And the seven angels, who had the seven trumpets, prepared themselves to sound them.**

¶ **Prepared themselves**) so that each one, when his turn came in the order, could be heard immediately. 5. The trumpets and the bowls are like each other in their number—seven—and in that they strike the earth, the sea, the rivers, the sun, etc., in the same sequence one after another: but in many more respects they are distinct. The trumpets themselves are called something different than the bowls: and all seven bowls belong under the single trumpet of the seventh angel. The trumpets strike the world itself: the bowls strike the Beast, as it has seized worldly government under a spiritual mask <note>original: "geistlichen Masque"; referring to a religious authority exercising political power</note>. The former take a very wide detour, and in their progress are encompassed in long periods of time <note>original: "Zeitläuffe"</note>: the latter run their course quickly, without any indication of time. The former hit a third part of each target; the bowl hits the whole, sharply and swiftly. The former indicate the damage that so many enemies do under divine permission <note>original: "göttlicher Verhängniß"; the theological concept of God allowing events to unfold according to His will even if they involve the actions of enemies</note>: the latter indicate divine retribution and vengeance against those same enemies. In the former, the language is much more figurative <note>original: "verblümt"; literally "flowery," meaning veiled or allegorical</note> than in the latter: for **GOD** performs miracles through these bowls, whereas the enemies do not perform them under the trumpets: and the further one proceeds in the book, the more the clarity increases. VIII. 8. 9. And the — [was] destroyed.

...given: <note>This sentence fragment completes a thought from the previous page regarding geographical interpretations.</note> one must not look merely at the edge of this island, but rather at the whole world and the language of Scripture. In this context, **the sea**—especially when contrasted with the land—or the "islands in the sea," is understood as the <term>Occident</term> <note>The West; from the Latin *occidens*.</note> or **Europe**, particularly its southern parts or the vast Roman territory within it.

2. The seven mountains upon which *Babylon* <note>In apocalyptic literature, "Babylon" is a common pseudonym for Rome.</note> sits are literal mountains; however, the language used here is figurative. In this sense, a mountain signifies a great power and a multitude of peoples, as seen in <term>Jeremiah 51:25</term> <note>Where the prophet refers to Babylon as a "destroying mountain."</note>. Thus, what is indicated here is the invasion of the Roman Empire by foreign peoples, the so-called <term>Barbarians</term>. Around the year 250, the bellicose <term>Goths</term> invaded the Roman Empire, and from that point on, the <term>Migration</term> <note>original: "Migration"; referring to the *Völkerwanderung* or the Great Migration Period (c. 300–500 AD) of Germanic and other tribes.</note> and the incursions of such peoples did not cease until they had, so to speak, incorporated themselves into the Roman Empire.

3. **The fire** represented the wrath of these warring peoples, which was repeatedly provoked by the Romans themselves.

4. This multitude of people, resembling a fiery mountain, was indeed "swallowed up" by the sea—as they suffered many a massive defeat—but the sea, or rather the Roman Empire, was the true target, along with the creatures in the sea and the ships.

435] VIII, 10. 11.
Ee 2

And they—had been.
It cannot be expressed how many people, especially in Alexandria, throughout all of Egypt, and in the neighboring lands, were consumed by the fury of the Arians <note>Arianism was a major Christological heresy that claimed Jesus was a created being, subordinate to God the Father; it caused massive civil and religious strife.</note>, and what great disruptions arose in the secular government because of it. Yet the situation in Africa, on account of the foreign peoples, remained much better than elsewhere in the Roman Empire, until the governor Bonifacius—whose wife was deeply devoted to the Arian heresy and was a kinswoman of Geiseric <note>original: "Genferici"</note>, the King of the Vandals—was slandered before the Empress Placidia <note>Galla Placidia (388–450 AD), mother of Valentinian III and a powerful regent of the Western Roman Empire.</note> by his rival Aetius under this very pretext. Bonifacius was then moved to entice those people who were devoted to the Arian doctrine to come there. Thus, the Vandals, under Geiseric, became masters of Africa in the year 428 and established their own kingdom, which lasted until the year 533. It is terrible to consider what tribulations and persecutions the people in Africa, and especially the Orthodox <note>The "Orthodox" here refers to those adhering to the Nicene Creed, which opposed Arianism.</note>, suffered under these Vandal kings. # The Ninth Chapter

## The 1st Verse

And the fifth angel sounded his trumpet, and I saw a star fallen from heaven to the earth, and to him was given the key to the shaft of the abyss.

¶ **A star**) This star that has fallen from heaven to the earth is located in the invisible realm. Consider this comparison: the third Woe is caused by the dragon cast out of heaven by Michael; the second Woe breaks in when a voice calls from the horns of the golden altar, "Release!", and the four angels at the Euphrates are set free; the first Woe is brought here by the angel of the abyss, which abyss this star fallen from heaven to earth opens. Just as Michael, and the one who calls from the horns of the golden altar, are holy, so too is this star a holy angel. See also the Introduction, page 73. Thus, this star is significantly different from the star Wormwood <note>original: "Absinthus"</note> in chapter 8, verse 11.

<header>And the fifth—given. IX. 1.</header>

¶ **From heaven**) This refers to heaven itself, in contrast to the earth, which contains the abyss within and beneath it.

¶ **Fallen**) John did not see the star in the act of falling, but rather as it had already fallen. It had fallen with speed and of its own free will, without any forced tumbling, toward the commission assigned to it. This "falling" does not prove that it is an evil angel. Consider the passage in Matthew 21:44: "on whomsoever this stone shall fall." <note>original: "auf welchen dieser Stein fället"</note> Falling is something more than merely descending, but it is less than being "cast down" <note>original: "herabgeworfen werden"</note>; nevertheless, not only the latter but also the former is said of Satan in chapter 12, verses 9 and 12.

¶ **Upon the earth**) This is not mentioned later regarding the sixth angel who held the trumpet; nor is it said of Michael.

¶ **It was given**) only after his falling. By contrast, the angel in chapter 20, verse 1 already possessed the key to the abyss during his descent.

¶ **To him**) that is, to the star.

¶ **The shaft of the abyss**) The abyss is frequently mentioned in this book, and always in such a way that the word never signifies the sea. The Beast first rises out of the sea, and finally out of the abyss. The sea is set in contrast to the earth, and the abyss is set in contrast to heaven. The abyss is

¶ **At the great river Euphrates**) This river, already famous in the time of Moses (Genesis 2:14), later became the border of the Promised Land, and later still the eastern border of the Roman Empire. There is no reason to seek a figurative <note>original: *verblümten Verstand*; literally "flowery understanding," referring to an allegorical or metaphorical interpretation</note> meaning here: it refers specifically to the well-known river in the East <note>original: *Orient*</note>, as also in Chapter 16:12. A city can borrow the name of another (such as Sodom or Babylon) because of their similarities, as seen in Chapter 11:8 (where the word **spiritually** expressly indicates a figurative meaning) and Chapter 14:8. However, one cannot find such an example regarding watercourses. A city can arise in the place of another, but a river remains the same from one era to the next.

### And it — of men. IX. 15. [469

This second woe, as also later the beginning of the third woe under the dragon, certainly has its place between the cessation of the locusts and the rising of the beast out of the sea. It occurred precisely at the time when the Saracen <term>Saracen: A term used in the Middle Ages for Arab Muslims, derived from Greek and Latin sources.</term> cavalry was most violently engaged in killing: that is, from the first Caliph, Abu Bakr, until their attacks on the city of Rome failed under Leo IV. The 212 1/2 years might most fittingly be reckoned from the year 634 to 847.

# And the—thefts. IX. 20. 21.

¶ **Idols**) Already around the year 590, people began to venerate images, and although honest people zealously opposed it, the images gradually became idols. The **Saracens** <note>A term used in the Middle Ages for Arabs or Muslims.</note>, through whom the plagues were carried out, held this in abomination, just as the **Turks** do to this day. The dispute over these images was driven to great heights in the Eastern and Western lands <note>original: "Morgen= und Abendlåndern"</note>, and lasted through the entire "Second Woe"; for this reason, the eighth century in particular is called the <term>Seculum Iconoclasticum</term> <note>The "Iconoclastic Century," a period of intense conflict over the use of religious images.</note>. In the year 787, **image-worship** <term>Bilderdienst</term> was confirmed at the <term>Second Council of Nicaea</term> <note>original: "Concilio Nicæno II"</note>. As the Second Woe was nearing its end, the last and most vehement zealot against images, Emperor **Theophilus**, died in the year 842. His widow **Theodora** immediately confirmed image-worship, to which she had previously been most zealously devoted: and although **Bardanes** was opposed to this abomination, it was nonetheless reaffirmed in Constantinople at a Council in the years 863 and 871. The Greeks have remained with this practice from that time until this very day, and they annually observe the so-called **Feast of Orthodoxy** <term>Fest der Orthodoxie</term> on the first Sunday of Lent because of **Theodora’s** decree. In the times of **Charlemagne** <note>original: "Caroli M." (Carolus Magnus)</note> and for a while thereafter, testimony was given against it in the **West** <term>Occident</term>: yet the veneration of images has also maintained the upper hand in the Roman Church, and continues to be defended and carried on even in these otherwise so rational times. Artificial makeup does not prevent—

2. Just as not every murderer is also a **sorcerer**, **adulterer**, and **thief**, so too is not every one of these an adorer of **demons** and **idols**. One should not neglect to consider the Introduction § 10 here.

¶ **Another mighty angel**) This is a created angel: for he does not swear by himself in verse 6 <note>In theology, only God swears by Himself; an angel must swear by a higher power.</note>. More proof is to be found in chapter VIII. 3. An even more powerful, and yet still created angel appears in chapter XVIII. 1. However, each one shows himself with a brilliance appropriate to his message and duty.

2. This mighty angel with the opened little book is, as "another," distinguished from that mighty angel mentioned in Chapter V. 2 regarding the sealed book. Between these two, no other mighty angel is mentioned.

3. Thus, this angel is not a human being. His duty is much too great for that: compare Daniel XII. 7, just as he also gives the little book here to John, the contents of which humans first learn through John.

4. A scroll has flight without wings in Zechariah 5:1; an arrow in Psalm 91:5; a sword in Ezekiel 32:10; a cloud in Isaiah 60:8. Conversely, wings are also given to other things for purposes other than flight, as in Isaiah 6:2 <note>In this passage, seraphim use their wings to cover their faces and feet out of reverence, rather than for flying.</note>. In many appearances, the angels were without wings: Genesis 28:12 <note>Jacob’s ladder, where angels ascend and descend.</note>, Judges 6:21–22, Judges 13:21, and Hebrews 13:2. ¶ **And the rainbow)** This is the lovely sign of divine grace. This attribute also applies to a created angel. The woman in Chapter 12:1 is described even more gloriously <note>Referencing the "woman clothed with the sun," often interpreted as the Church or Mary.</note>.

¶ **And his face, like the sun)** The righteous will shine like the sun, according to Matthew 13:43; thus, such a thing can certainly be attributed to this created angel as well. It sounds even more magnificent when spoken of the Lord Jesus in chapter 1:16: *His face was like the sun shining in its strength.*

¶ **His feet like pillars of fire)** This signifies taking a stand <note>original: "Posto zu fassen"; a phrase derived from military terminology meaning to take up a position.</note> in an invincible manner wherever he placed his feet.

2. The cloud and the fire are found here together. Compare Exodus 13:21 <note>original: "2 Mos. XIII. 21."; refers to the pillar of cloud and fire that guided the Israelites in the wilderness.</note>.

### Verse 2

And he had in his hand a little book, opened, and he set his right foot upon the sea, and the left upon the earth.

¶ **In his hand**) namely, in the left: for with the right hand he swore, as seen in verse 5. It is phrased similarly in Psalm 91:7: **Though a thousand fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand**: in which case the **side** refers to the left side. Likewise, in Judges 5:26: **She reached out with her (left) hand for the tent peg, and with her right for the workman's hammer.** The angel stood with his right foot on the sea, toward the evening <note>In traditional orientation, "evening" refers to the West, where the sun sets.</note>, and with his left on the earth, toward the morning <note>The "morning" refers to the East, where the sun rises.</note>, so that his face was directed toward midday <note>The "midday" refers to the South.</note>. Therefore, John could easily take the little book from the left hand of the angel. For Patmos <note>The island where John received his visions.</note> lies close to Asia.

2. The sealed book was initially in the right hand of **Him** who sat on the throne; from Him the Little Lamb <note>Refers to Jesus Christ, the Lamb of God, as depicted in Revelation 5.</note> took the book and opened the seven seals. Now, the little book is given by the angel to John—and indeed, already opened—to be eaten. This little book contains within itself the *remanet* <term>remanet: a Latin term meaning "the remnant" or "that which remains"</term>, or what was left over from that previous book. ### X. 4. And when the — do not write.

2. How accurately, certainly, and specifically everything must have been impressed upon the minds of the prophets, since, for example, John grasped the things spoken by the seven thunders so correctly and swiftly that he would have been able to write them down, even though he was not permitted to do so.

¶ **A Voice**) From the beginning of the book, the Lord Jesus himself so often commands John to write (Chapters 1, 2, 3), and thus it is undoubtedly also his voice that commands John to write in other places, yet here forbids the writing, while on the other hand commanding him to take the little book. Here, John does not report without reason that he heard the speech and received the command to seal it. Thus, we may at least reflect in general on what the office of these seven thunders might be—namely, that they promote the praise of God in the most powerful way.

## Verse 6.

> And he swore by Him who lives forever and ever, who created heaven and what is in it, and the earth and what is in it, and the sea and what is in it: There shall be no more delay <note>original: "Frist"; often translated as "time" or "interval," meaning there will be no more waiting before the end arrives</note>, 7. but in the days of the voice of the seventh angel, when he shall sound his trumpet, the mystery of **God** shall be finished, as he has declared the gospel to his servants the prophets.

<header>X.6.7. And he swore — Prophets.</header>

2. The trumpets of the six previous angels passed without an oath, for they only had to clear the path for the Kingdom of **God**: but now the trumpet of the seventh angel alone is assured beforehand with a most precious oath. The **LORD** lets his angel swear, and he will not repent of it: His and His Anointed's kingdom is an eternal kingdom. *chapter XI. 15.* <note>Revelation 11:15: "The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Messiah."</note>

¶ By Him who lives) By the life of **God**, **God** himself, as well as angels and men, swear. Before Him, who lives eternally, a thousand years are but a *Non-Time* <note>original: "Non-chronus"; a technical term in this author's system for a period of time shorter than a "chronus," specifically 10/11ths of a "chronus"</note>, indeed even a *Time* <note>original: "Chronus"; in this prophetic system, a "Chronus" is a specific unit of time, calculated by some scholars like Bengel as 1,111 years</note>, like the shortest day, as if it were about to pass away, and like a watch in the night. *Psalm XC. 4.* <note>Psalm 90:4</note>

¶ Who created) The creation of all things is a primary ground for the honor, praise, and power that belong to **God**: *chapter IV. 11.* <note>Revelation 4:11</note> and the creation of heaven, the earth, and the sea, and all that is within them, is a primary reason why the enemies—who rage for a while in heaven, on the sea, and on the earth—shall nevertheless not carry it on for long, but must give way. Here, John's narrative is supplemented by the angel's words. The preceding sweetness flowed from the good news found in Chapter XI, 1, 15ff; the bitterness arose from the third woe <term>The "third woe" represents the final series of divine judgments preceding the end of the age.</term> and from the delay of the "Good"; and the subsequent sweetness flowed from the "Good" that arrives after the third woe has passed.

¶ **When I ate it)** By this, the short duration of the bitterness is expressed, situated as it is between the far-reaching periods of sweetness.

¶ **Peoples and nations and languages**
**and many kings**) The word **many** stands at the end in the original text <note>The "original text" refers to the Greek Source (the Textus Receptus or similar manuscript) of the New Testament.</note>, and is therefore to be construed either with the **peoples and nations and languages**, or rather—because this word **many** does not appear in **chapters XI. 9. and XVII. 15.** or in other places—only with the **kings**, who are also only mentioned in this place alongside the **peoples and nations and languages**. ¶ **Quickly)** The beginning of the **third woe** <note>original: *Weh*; refers to the final three judgments in Revelation, signaled by the last three trumpet blasts.</note> is found in chapter 12:12. **Answer:** From the passage in chapter 8:13, where it said, "Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth," the focus is primarily on the third woe, as this is the only woe in which those "who dwell on the earth" are again explicitly mentioned. Between the first and third woe, there is a span of 358 years, and thus it is said with every right that the two woes come thereafter. On the other hand, the span between the second and third woe is not even a third of that previous duration, and thus the third woe now comes "quickly." Before the passing of the second woe, great things occurred that gave the matter a swift course.

<header>XI. 15. And the—eternities.</header>

¶ **The seventh)** The trumpet of the seventh angel is the most significant of all. All that preceded was a preparation for this one, and the trumpet itself was given to the angel quite early on in chapter 8:2. It encompasses the greater part of the time that has elapsed from John <note>The Apostle John, the traditional author of Revelation.</note> until our own day, as well as all times yet to come.

¶ **Angel)** A bold new interpreter <note>The author likely refers to a contemporary biblical commentator or scholar.</note> suggests that Gabriel is the strong angel mentioned in chapter 5:2 and 10:1. However, in chapter 10:1, it is another **strong** angel, specifically in contrast to the one in chapter 5:2. Nevertheless, Gabriel undoubtedly has his duties in the Revelation, just as he did in the books of Daniel and Luke; and he might well be this seventh trumpeting angel. This is what occurs so often in the Psalms: *Dominus regnavit* <note>original: "Dominus regnavit"; The Lord reigns / The Lord has become King.</note>: **The LORD is King**, or, **has become King**. <header>XI. 17. And — accepted.</header>

### Giving thanks
The thanksgiving <note>original: "Danksagung"</note> actually occurs for the reward, which is considered hereafter: and such a reward must be solely a **reward of grace** <term>reward of grace: A theological concept (German: Gnadenlohn) meaning a reward given not because it is earned by merit, but out of God's free favor.</term>, because they give thanks for it. Included within this thanksgiving, because it is joined with adoration, is also the praise that is due to the divine Majesty who reveals Himself here so gloriously. Likewise, it contains the power of a petition—where such a thing might be necessary—for the fulfillment of those desired things for which they give such great thanks **in advance** <note>original Latin: "in antecessum"</note>.

### Almighty
This is a royal title, yet one belonging to **God** alone: **Almighty** <note>original Greek: "Pantocrator," meaning the one who holds all things in His power</note>, the one who holds all things in His power as the sole Ruler. This designation was found in **ch. I. 8** and **IV. 8**, and only now reappears under the trumpet of the seventh angel, specifically seven times: here, and in **ch. XV. 3, XVI. 7, 14, XIX. 6, 15, XXI. 22**.

Previously, the **LORD** was called several times **who was, and who is, and who is to come**, in the song of praise of the four living creatures; or, in the title which the **LORD** gave Himself and which John gave Him: **who is, and who was, and who is to come**. 559] **And those who — destroyed. XI, 18.**

...in this verse, the progress and outcome of what occurs under the trumpet of the seventh angel are described. The beginning, progress, and outcome are linked together without interruption and, together, span a great period of time.

¶ **And (is the time of the dead)** In apocalyptic language—especially when a heavenly voice is speaking—the "dead" are sometimes not only those who have actually died, but also those who still bear the image of the earthly man and have not yet overcome death. Consequently, this refers collectively to all those who have not yet attained immortality in their bodies (Revelation 14:13; 20:5, 12). The Prince of Life <note>A title for Jesus Christ, based on Acts 3:15.</note> spoke in the same manner in Matthew 8:22 <note>"Let the dead bury their dead."</note>, and in this sense, Adam died on the day of his transgression (Genesis 2:17 <note>original: "1 Mos. II. 17." — The First Book of Moses is the traditional German name for Genesis.</note>). Indeed, our body is also "dead" because of sin (Romans 8:10). Thus, the "dead" here, whose time for reward has come, are the very same multitude usually called the **living and the dead**; and this way of speaking is very appropriate here. For: 1. Those who are giving thanks here speak of themselves and others like them who had died. 2. As for the living, things could well wait a good while longer for their sake; but for the dead, it has already been delayed a long time. It is primarily "time" for their sake. 3. The dead are an incomparably larger multitude than the living:

<header>And those who — destroyed. 11:18.</header>

In this verse, the progress and the outcome of what occurs under the trumpet of the seventh angel are described. The beginning, progress, and outcome are linked together without interruption and together occupy a great span of time.

¶ **And (it is the time of the dead)** In apocalyptic language, especially when a heavenly voice takes the lead, "the dead" are sometimes not only those who have physically died, but also those who still bear the image of the earthly human and have not yet overcome death; consequently, this includes all those who have not yet attained immortality with their bodies, *Chapter 14:13; 20:5, 12.* In the same way, the Prince of Life <note>A common title for Jesus Christ, derived from Acts 3:15.</note> himself spoke in *Matthew 8:22*, and in such a sense **Adam** died on the day of his transgression, *Genesis 2:17*. Indeed, even our body is "dead" because of sin, *Romans 8:10*. Thus, the "dead" here, whose time of reward has come, are the very same multitude that one otherwise calls "the living and the dead"; and this manner of speaking is very appropriate here. For: 1. Those who give thanks here speak of themselves and others like them who had died. 2. As far as the living are concerned, it might well wait a good while longer for their sake; but for the dead, it has already been waiting a long time. It is primarily "time" on their account. 3. The dead are an incomparably greater multitude than the living:

Therefore, the "God-fearing" are so often mentioned (Psalm 66:16).

### And it—twelve stars. XII. 1.

In these chapters, the misery is described, and from this point onward, the enemies are portrayed. In the tribulations contained in previous chapters, the authors <note>original: "Urheber"; those responsible for or the source of the suffering.</note> of those hardships were described alongside the events themselves. However, regarding the enemies described in the following sections—the dragon, the beasts, and the prostitute—the misery they cause is also introduced.

4. There is something, however, that should not be so strictly confined to the sequence of the text. Here, the woman in labor and the dragon are described, and each of these two descriptions can be understood as a logical statement <note>original: "Enunciation"; a formal declaration or proposition.</note> consisting of its (1) **Subject** <note>original: "Subjecto"; the person or thing being described.</note> and (2) **Predicate** <note>original: "Prædicato"; the action or quality attributed to the subject.</note>:

(1) **A Woman**, who was surrounded by the **sun**, **moon**, and **stars**, and was pregnant:

(2) she gave birth to a male son.

Likewise:

(1) A seven-headed **Dragon**, with seven diadems <note>original: "Hauptbinden"; literally "head-bands," referring to the royal crowns or diadems mentioned in the biblical text.</note>:

(2) he fought against the **Woman**.

And again:

(1) The great **Dragon**, the ancient **Serpent**, the so-called **Devil**, and **Satan**, who seduced the entire world and accused the saints:

(2) he fought, did not prevail, and was cast down to the **earth**.

One can view the Subject in these passages as a summary of many older,

### And there — twelve stars. XII. 1.
<meta>catchword: the</meta>

¶ (**In the heaven**) Here and in verse 3, the properly so-called heaven is to be understood, as also in verses 7, 8, 12: in contrast to the earth and the sea. verses 9, 12, 13. It is precisely the heaven in which afterwards the seven angels with their bowls appear as **another) great and wondrous sign.** ch. XV. 1.

¶ (**A Woman**) This woman is the congregation <note>original: "Gemeine"; refers to the community of believers or the Church.</note> of God and Christ, as the same originally and primarily sprang from Israel, and yet also from the Gentiles <note>original: "Heiden"; refers to non-Jewish nations.</note>, was planted, built up, spread toward the East and West <note>original: "gegen Morgen und Abend"; literally "toward morning and evening," a common idiom for East and West.</note> and preserved, and shall in the future become much more respectable, especially then, when the natural branches are grafted back into their own olive tree. <note>A reference to the theology of Romans 11, regarding the eventual restoration of the Jewish people to God's favor.</note> Great attention is paid here to Israel. For Israel is the root: many Israelites are believers who no longer know their own descent from the fathers themselves: from those who passed away in unbelief from one generation to another: their descendants will be converted. # XII. 5. And she gave birth — Throne.
## 2.
<meta>catchword: This</meta>

is nonetheless a testimony—at least before the conscience of all those who have held and still hold the matter to be either truthful or only possible—that the Roman Church is by no means the mother of the Shepherd of all nations <note>The author is refuting the idea that the Roman Catholic Church is the "Woman" of Revelation 12, likely referencing the "Pope Joan" legend mentioned on the previous page to argue that the institutional church is not the source of Christ’s millennial rule.</note>.

### Verse 6

> And the woman fled into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God, that they should feed her there a thousand two hundred and sixty days.

¶ **And the woman**, etc. Here, various things are to be considered. The **wilderness** is without doubt on earth; and thus the woman herself, as we previously established, is also on earth, even though she was seen in heaven. And indeed, the wilderness is very large in contrast to the land of Israel, but here this word signifies that part of the earth where the woman, after she had given birth, gradually found a new dwelling place—namely, certain European lands. This is because Asia and Africa were in the hands of the **Saracens** <note>A medieval term for Arabs or Muslims.</note> and **Turks**, and in those regions there was no new refuge for the woman at all; rather, she had to flee from there. It does not say here, "into *a* wilderness," as in Chapter XVII:3.
