### XII. 6. And — sixty Days.

The conclusion of the 1260 days of the **Woman in the Wilderness** <note>In the Book of Revelation, the "Woman" is traditionally interpreted by Protestant scholars as the true Church fleeing persecution.</note> is in itself something significant, although the conclusion of the **three and a half times** <note>German: *vierthalb Zeiten*. For a long time before the **Reformation**, nothing greater happened to the Church than the Reformation itself: and nothing greater follows after it until the enemies are cleared away one after another, and the three and a half times are replaced by the **thousand years** <note>The Millennium, or the promised thousand-year reign of Christ on earth.</note>. Thus, the 1260 days of the Woman have a good conclusion, and her 1. 2. ½ times have an even better one; the former at the Reformation, the latter at the dawn of the thousand years.

These are two milestones between which the Church occupies an **intermediate state** for a time—a state that is better than before, but is not yet what it is destined to become. The former should move us to gratitude, and the latter to patience; both, however, should move us to humility on all sides. XII. 7. 8. And it—the heaven.

3. **Michael** the Archangel is a created angel. See **Daniel** 10:13, 21 and 12:1. During the dispute with the devil over the body of **Moses**, he did not dare to pass a blasphemous judgment against him, but spoke: "May the **Lord** rebuke you" (**Epistle of Jude**, verse 9). This modesty, which is appropriate only for a created being—especially when compared with the passage in **2 Peter** 2:11—certainly indicates a created angel; and such a virtue is even contained within his very name. For **Michael** means, "Who is like **God**?" <note>The Hebrew name *Mikha'el* is a rhetorical question: *Mi* (Who) *kha* (is like) *El* (God)? It serves as a humble declaration of God's uniqueness.</note> and thus encompasses this noble angel's humility and his distance from all self-exaltation, as well as the *sum total* <note>original: *Summam*</note> of his service and the guiding principle of his duties. **Satan** wanted to be like **God**; conversely, **Michael** proclaims: "Who is like **God**?" Who? Not the Archangel, and certainly not Satan. Since **Michael** is certainly the proper name of a created angel, we cannot consider the **Michael** in the Revelation to be the **Lord Jesus Christ** Himself. A proper name <note>original: *nomen proprium*</note> is given, accepted, and used specifically so that a distinction might be made; and if **God's** Son had this name **Michael**, it would be a divine name that could never be given to a created angel anywhere.

4. Yet this **Michael**, the great prince (**Daniel** 12:1), has his angels, just as the **Dragon** also has his angels.

### IV. One can easily sin against others who are diligent in this matter.

He who loves and practices Christian **gravity** <term>Gravität</term> <note>In this context, a sense of dignity, seriousness, and moral weight in one's conduct.</note> and **fairness** <term>Billigkeit</term> <note>Also implies equity or a reasonable, balanced judgment.</note> does not measure everyone else by his own standard; rather, he recognizes the **diversity of gifts** and, in the interpretation of prophecy, makes a careful distinction between the main point and secondary matters. 

On the other hand, superficial and flighty minds do not wish to conduct an investigation, but only want to know quickly and plainly "what time it is" <note>A metaphor for wanting to know exactly when the "end times" or specific biblical milestones will occur.</note>. They might seize upon a date <term>Termin</term> conjectured by someone and cling to it entirely; then, depending on whether that date passes without event or remains far off, an interpreter—even if he had spoken with the greatest caution and modesty—must be either a "prophet" or a "fool" in their eyes. 

If a certain circumstance does come to pass, they make far too much of it; if it fails to appear, they believe they have reason enough to destroy everything at once, or even say, "Aha! We are glad to see that!" Indeed, if someone who claims to be a **prophet** fails in even a single small point, he makes himself worthy of rejection; however, in the work of an **interpreter** <term>Ausleger</term>, something deficient can certainly slip in without undermining the main substance of his explanation.

<header>XII. 14. And there — of the serpent</header>
<page-type>text</page-type>

### The 14th Verse.

> And to the woman were given two wings of a great eagle, that she might fly into the wilderness, into her place, where she is nourished for a time, and times, and half a time, from the face of the serpent.

¶ *And there — to her place*) The eagle is commonly called the king among the birds, and it is an image of great **potentates** <note>Powerful rulers or monarchs.</note> and kings. Thus, in **Ezekiel 17:3** <note>original: *Ezech. XVII. 3.*</note>, the great eagle is described: great of wings, long-winged, full of feathers, which had diverse colors. And in verse 7: another great eagle, great of wings and many feathers. By the latter, the King of **Egypt** is understood, and by the former, the King of **Babylon** <note>original: *Babel*</note>. This first eagle, however, is presented as much greater than the other, and is described as such an eagle that had no equal at that time. Since it is also said here, "the wings of the great eagle," it is to be understood as the mightiest power from which the Christian Church enjoyed protection and advancement after the arrival of the **third woe** <note>In the Book of Revelation, the "woes" represent periods of great tribulation; the third woe is often associated with the final judgment or the establishment of God's kingdom.</note>. That was, then, the **Imperial Power** <note>The Holy Roman Empire; the author likely identifies the "great eagle" with the eagle on the imperial coat of arms.</note>.

2. Mention was already made in the 6th verse of a place in the wilderness, and that same verse has a great similarity with this 14th verse. Although many **commentators** <note>original: *Ausleger*; scholars who interpret the Bible.</note> consider both verses to be entirely the same, there is nevertheless a manifold difference present, which we must now discuss.

<header>XII. 14. And there — of the serpent.</header>

In the same way, the following follow one after another:
1) The beginning of the 1260 days;
2) The beginning of the **short time**;
3) The beginning of the **three and a half times** <note>original: *vierthalb Zeiten*; an archaic German expression meaning "the fourth is half," or 3.5.</note>.

And these are three periods of time, of which the third corresponds with the second in that both are expressed in **times** <term>original: καιρους (kairous); meaning specific, appointed seasons or periods</term>; and it corresponds even more with the first, in that both are attributed to the **Woman** <note>In this context, the Woman is usually interpreted as the Church or the people of God.</note>. It is true that under the first woe, the five months of the **locusts** <note>A reference to the plague in Revelation 9.</note> are mentioned twice, and under the third woe the times of the **Beast** are also expressed twice—namely, through the 42 months and through the number 666. However, it does not follow from this that the Woman’s 1260 days and her three and a half times must also be exactly the same thing. This is especially true since the "short time" begins between these two periods. By contrast, no other period of time begins between the two ways of expressing the time of the locusts, nor between the two ways of expressing the time of the Beast. Furthermore, under the third woe, it is sufficient that the time of the Beast is expressed twice. Even the "short time" of the third woe itself—which strikes the earth and the sea—is expressed simply. This short time aligns with the greatest part of the **non-time** <term>original: Non-chroni; referring to Revelation 10:6, often translated as "there shall be time no longer" or "no more delay"</term>, which the angel standing on the sea and the earth swore by; and hereafter, in Chapter 20:3, it may have some connection with the **little season**.

And it was exactly then that the **Turks** became powerful over the **Saracens** <note>The Arab-Muslim dynasties that the Turks eventually supplanted as the dominant power in the Islamic world.</note>, and they advanced ever further into Asia, to the great disadvantage of the **Eastern Empire** <note>original: morgenländischen Kaiserthums; the Byzantine Empire.</note>, although at times the Emperors themselves or their generals offered forceful resistance. In the year 1071, they took the Greek Emperor **Romanus Diogenes** prisoner; he himself was treated very gently by **Sultan Axan** <note>Sultan Alp Arslan, who defeated the Byzantines at the Battle of Manzikert.</note> and released, but all the provinces still remaining in Asia were completely lost. In particular, the so-called **Crusades** <note>original: Creuzfahrten.</note> belong here; although they were not of much use in other respects, they nevertheless held back the flood in Asia and swallowed much of it. In this regard, the orders founded for the same purpose—the **Knights of St. John**, the **Knights Templar**, and the **Knights of the Cross** <note>Likely the Teutonic Knights or other military-religious orders whose mission was to defend the Holy Land.</note>—also did their part and in some cases still do. The first Crusade lasted from the year 1096 to 1099.

**The Beast is a spiritual-secular power that opposes the Kingdom of Christ.**

Scripture is accustomed to representing great powers under the images and names of various animals, such as a bear, a ram, etc. <note>These are references to the visions in the Book of Daniel, which use animal imagery to represent historical empires.</note> In this, His Revelation, Jesus Christ is both a little Lamb and a Lion; by contrast, Satan is a serpent and a dragon. ### XIII. 1. And I saw — Blasphemy.
<meta>catchword: D</meta>

**Prophet** are interpreted by some together as worldly powers, or by others together as dark, spiritual powers. The truth walks in the middle. The Dragon is explicitly named the Devil and Satan: but just as the locusts are under Abaddon, and the riders are under the four released angels <note>These references are to Revelation 9, where supernatural plagues are led by specific spiritual entities.</note>, so under Satan are the Beast and the False Prophet, who come from the human race: and this is clearly evident from Chapter XIX, 20, where the two are thrown **alive** into the lake of fire. ## Proposition III.

### The Beast is connected with the city of Rome in the most precise and particular way.

This is made sufficiently clear in the 17th Chapter <note>The author refers to Revelation 17, which describes the Whore of Babylon sitting upon a scarlet beast, often interpreted by Reformation-era theologians as a critique of Rome.</note>: and in that same 17th Chapter, much will occur that elucidates this proposition, as well as the preceding first and partly the following propositions. ## Proposition IV.

### XIII. 1. And I saw — Blasphemy [672]

The successors [of the early church leaders] received many honors, protection, wealth, and worldly goods—even dominion over land and people—through their own virtues, and at times through their pleas and entreaties, as well as through the favor, misguided devotion, and lack of caution among the powerful. ### XIII. 1. And I saw — Blasphemy

The former is killed and thrown into the fire; the latter is thrown **alive** into the lake of fire.

<center>And this — great power. XIII. 2.</center>

This is the name *Papa*, or Pope; not as it was previously used out of a general respect for bishops, but in that very specific and exalted sense which the Pope himself and his worshippers have assigned to him—as a "most holy father," and consequently as both a priest and a king—using so many languages to indicate all the prerogatives attributed to him. He is also called, though not as frequently, *Pontifex maximus* <note>original Latin: "Greatest Priest"</note>, the greatest priest. This title carried significant weight even in pagan Rome, but it refers only to the priesthood; by contrast, the word "Pope" encompasses the entire dignity of the supreme Father on Earth. Among the <term>Dictatus Papae</term> <note>A collection of 27 statements of powers claimed by Pope Gregory VII in 1075, asserting absolute papal authority</note> and authoritative decrees of Gregory, the following two stand together: *Quod illius (Papæ) solius nomen in ECCLESIIS recitetur: quod unicum est nomen in MUNDO.* <note>original Latin: "That his [the Pope's] name alone shall be recited in the churches: that it is the only name in the world."</note> This means that the Pope's name alone should be proclaimed and named in both the churches and in the secular world. Thus, the Church and the world are meant to call this single individual "Father" upon the earth.

### XIII. 3. And one — Beast

...until 1176, there were five schisms and at least as many **antipopes** <note>original: "Gegenpäbste"; rival claimants to the papacy who were not recognized by the Roman Catholic Church as legitimate.</note> (many of whom had a better cause than the Pope who was considered legitimate). These were also partly installed and supported by the Emperors themselves. These conflicts were very dangerous to the papal kingdom (Matthew 12:25) <note>Matthew 12:25: "Every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation."</note>, as **Platina** <note>Bartolomeo Platina (1421–1481), a Renaissance humanist and author of a famous history of the Popes.</note> judges that the Roman Church was nearly overturned by the antipopes of **Alexander III**.

Another severe symptom was II. the resistance of the secular lords in Rome against the Pope, as they would by no means allow him to be a secular ruler, and especially not one over them. That which the Great Men in Rome had already attempted in the 10th century under **Stephen**, they also allowed to be seen under **Gregory VII**, and brought to fruition under **Innocent II** in the 12th century. They did this by organizing the commonwealth <term>commonwealth: the public state or body politic; in this case, the Commune of Rome</term> in the ancient manner, using the years of the Senate as a calendar date, removing the Pope from the city government, and directing him to be content with the **tithe** <note>A one-tenth tax on income intended for the support of the church and clergy.</note> and to attend only to the duties of the episcopal office.

Regarding this, as **Panvinius** <note>Onofrio Panvinio (1529–1568), an Augustinian friar and historian who wrote extensively on Roman history and the papacy.</note> summarizes it briefly and well, **Innocent II** and **Celestine II** grieved themselves to death. **Lucius II**, when he attacked the **Capitol** <note>The Capitoline Hill, the historic seat of Rome's civil government.</note> and the Roman Senate within it with an armed force, was struck by a stone and died a few days later.

### XIII. 3. And one — after the Beast

The prophecy here does not aim at those earlier events. It begins with the emergence from the sea <note>Referring to Revelation 13:1, where the first Beast rises out of the sea, often interpreted by commentators of this era as the emergence of the Papacy from the "sea" of nations or historical chaos.</note>. We wish to note several circumstances in particular:

| Wound: | Recovery. |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Hildebrand** <note>Hildebrand of Sovana (c. 1015–1085), who reigned as Pope Gregory VII.</note> was deposed by the Emperor and by many bishops: | **Gregory** maintains his cause. |
| **Hildebrand** received an imperial **antipope** <term>antipope: a person who, in opposition to the one who is generally seen as the legitimately elected pope, makes a significant attempt to occupy the Holy See.</term>, and died as an exile: | **Gregory** appointed a successor, and it remained with him: That was **Victor III**. |

These might seem like small things in themselves, but life or death depends on slight circumstances even at the birth of such a person who, once grown, is destined to signify so much in the world. Had the imperial antipopes prevailed, then the Imperial Majesty might well have maintained its high right and power; but the Gregorian party <note>The faction supporting the reforms of Gregory VII, which sought to increase papal authority over secular rulers.</note> kept the upper hand. His opponents might continue to call him by his former name, **Hildebrand**, yet he remained **Gregory VII**. More than a hundred years later, the next Pope named **Gregory** was called not the seventh, but the eighth, and so the others followed in their sequence. What happened with **Gregory** himself was by far not the whole matter, but only a beginning, upon which, however, everything else hung.

### Verse 8.

And all who dwell on the earth will worship him, whose name is not written in the Book of Life of the Lamb, who allowed himself to be slaughtered, from the foundation of the world.

¶ **And all will worship him**) The manner of speaking in this verse is markedly different from several of the preceding ones. For the *tense* <note>original: "Tempus." The author is noting a shift from the historical past tense to the prophetic future tense.</note> changes: from *it was given to him* to *they will worship him*. Additionally, the *gender* <note>original: "Genus." In the Greek and German grammar, the author is highlighting a specific shift in how the "Beast" is referenced, moving to a masculine pronoun.</note> changes in the phrase *they will worship him*, where the masculine form sounds exactly as it does in *Chapter XVII, 11*. This indicates the universal worship of the Beast—which is yet to come and will rise to the highest degree—following which the "wonder" that is equivalent to worship is also described as a future event in *Chapter XVII, 8*. Nevertheless, the beginning of such an abomination is already found in this place, namely *Chapter XIII, 8*.

The temptation will be so universal and powerful that here, and in *Chapter XVII, 8*, eternal election <note>original: "ewige Erwählung." The theological doctrine of predestination, where God chooses His own before the world began.</note> is brought forward as a shield against it; compare *Matthew XXIV, 24* <note>"For false messiahs and false prophets will appear... to deceive, if possible, even the elect."</note>. <header>XIII, 10. If anyone — Holy</header>

### Verse 10.

> If anyone brings prisoners together <note>or "leads into captivity"</note>, he shall go into captivity: if anyone kills with the sword, he must be killed with the sword. Here is the patience and the faith of the saints.

¶ **If anyone**) Here, the text speaks of a <term>Talion: the law of retaliation, often known as "an eye for an eye."</term> or retribution. However, this is not referring to the retribution that will eventually strike the Beast and other enemies (which is described in other passages); rather, it refers to the retribution awaiting those who defend themselves against the Beast in a manner contrary to God’s intent. Nothing can ever be accomplished against the Beast through worldly power. May the Almighty give light and courage to those princes and powers in the Protestant Church, that they may never do too little or too much!

¶ **Brings prisoners together**) Helping people who are imprisoned for the sake of the truth to find their freedom in a Christian manner is a good work. But to herd prisoners together by force, with the intention of committing violence, is the path that leads to one's own captivity.

¶ **So he goes—be killed**) Such a person brings trouble upon himself, just as much as—or even more than—the saints who demonstrate patience and faith.

¶ **Here**) Similar requirements are found in verse 18, Chapter 14:12, and Chapter 17:9. One should particularly compare what we will note regarding Chapter 14:12.

### XIV. 1. And I—their foreheads.

Precisely those 144,000, who were mentioned in Chapter VII, verse 4, appear here once again. Previously, they were still in the world and were protected by the sealing on their foreheads against the harm <note>original: "Beleidigung"; in this 18th-century context, it refers to the "hurting" or "damaging" of the earth described in Revelation 7:2-3.</note> to the earth, the sea, etc., and against the plague of the locusts during the sounding of the trumpets. Now they find themselves in safety upon Mount Zion, and they have the name of the Lamb and the name of his Father written on their foreheads. They now have a much different appearance: for this reason, the text does not refer to them as "the" [specific] thousands, but as if starting anew, "one hundred forty-four thousand." In a similar way, the little word "the" is omitted in Chapter XVII, verse 3.

¶ **(His name and the name of his Father)** They are purchased as firstfruits <note>original: "Erstling"; the first and best portion of a harvest, consecrated to God.</note> to God and to the Lamb. Therefore, they have his name and his Father's name written on their foreheads (verse 4). The name of God and the name of the Lamb are announced together, as in Chapter III, verse 12; Ephesians V, verse 5; and Hebrews XII, verses 22–24. Whoever denies or confesses the Son also denies or confesses the Father (1 John II, verse 23).

2. Here it is called "the name," as in Chapter XXII, verse 4, and not "the seal." For the misery against which they were protected by the sealing is now entirely gone. Now they sing a new song (verse 3), and indeed even before those who overcome the Beast (Chapter XV, verse 2).

<header>And — playing harps. XIV. 2.</header>

3. The followers of the Beast have his name stamped upon their hand or forehead: but the saints have the name of the Lamb and the name of his Father written on their foreheads.

### Verse 2.

> And I heard a voice from heaven, like the voice of many waters, and like the voice of a great thunder: and the voice I heard was like that of harpists playing on their harps.

¶ (**A voice**) A similar voice, described in almost the same way, follows in Chapter XIX, verse 6.

¶ (**From heaven**) The voice was in heaven: from there John heard it.

¶ (**Waters etc.**) John perceived the voice more and more clearly: and for this reason, he describes it 1. through a comparison with waters and thunders: 2. even more closely, through the harps and the song.

¶ (**Of a great thunder**) Later it is called a "voice of mighty thunders" <note>original: "starker Donner"</note> in Chapter XIX, verse 6. This is a gradation <term>gradation: a rhetorical or logical sequence where the intensity or importance of the subject increases step-by-step</term>. The voice of the waters is, as can be gathered from the passage just mentioned, more delicate and brighter than the voice of the thunders: and thus the voice of the 144,000, as they are firstfruits <note>original: "Erstling"; refers to the first portion of the harvest dedicated to God, signifying their special status.</note> for the Lamb, might be compared with the waters, and as they are firstfruits for **GOD**, they might be compared with the thunders.

<header>XIV. 4. 5. These — they are blameless</header>

2. These are described by their character in relation to **GOD**, before His throne (verse 3); and now particularly (compare verse 1) in relation to the **Lamb** (verse 4); and then in relation to **GOD** and the **Lamb** together: **These were redeemed — they are blameless.** This description (like that in Chapter XX:6) sounds, in its figurative composition, almost like a song itself. For these two verses consist of six short phrases, of which the third and fourth express the **blessedness** and **glory** of this host, while the first two express their **prior good conduct** and **present excellent quality** of the body (verse 4), and the last two express their **prior good conduct** and **present excellent quality** of the spirit (verse 5). The twofold **good conduct** is that they did not defile themselves and spoke no lies—or rather, their freedom from abomination and lies (Chapter XXI:27). The two qualities are **purity** of the body and **blamelessness** of the soul.

¶ (**Who were not defiled with women; for they are young men.**) The Greek and Latin words, *virgins* <note>original: "παρθένοι" (parthenoi), "Virgines"</note>, are somewhat more conveniently suited for both sexes, but here the text actually pertains to the male sex, for "these" <note>original: "οὗτοι" (houtoi)</note> are described in the *masculine gender*, and are explicitly contrasted with the female sex. In the case of the former [women], one is accustomed to calling them **maidens** <note>original: "Jungfrauen"</note>, while in the case of the latter [men], one calls them **young men** <note>original: "Junge gesellen." In 18th-century German, this term refers to bachelors or unmarried young men, emphasizing their celibate state in this context.</note>.

Thus, the discussion here concerns **virginity** and **chastity** outside of marriage. The Greek word **to be defiled** <note>original: "μολυνομαι" (molynomai)</note> is very subtle and does not always signify a sinful defilement; however, in this context, it signifies exactly that which constitutes the difference between even a truly chaste marriage and an unmixed holiness of the body. **1 Corinthians VII. 34.** <note>This verse distinguishes between the married woman, who cares for the things of the world, and the unmarried woman, who cares for the things of the Lord and holiness in body and spirit.</note>

3. Yet, under such a designation, one understands an intact purity of the body—and thus chastity either outside of marriage or within marriage—as well as sobriety, moderation, and all those virtues through which the body itself becomes a partaker of sanctification, and without which, conversely, the single state is of no use. The literal sense here posits a natural **virginity**, but this is to be understood *metaphorically* <note>original: "per metaphoram"</note> or in a figurative way to mean the total sanctification of the body; and for some, the virtuous abstention from marriage is a part of such sanctification. For one cannot imagine that such a great number should be filled solely by holy **Israelites** of the single state, especially since among the Israelites very few remained without marriage. The little word "for" <note>original: "denn"</note> means, according to the Hebrew idiom, as much as "but" <note>original: "sondern"</note>; and here it carries a particular emphasis. 2. The angel flies at the time when the **Beast** still exists: thereafter follows the **Beast’s** <term>non-existence</term> <note>original: *Non-esse*. This refers to a period where the Beast is absent or inactive before its final ascent.</note>, its emergence from the abyss, and its departure into destruction: the thousand years when **Satan** is bound: the short period when he is released, alongside those thousand years when the **Saints** reign. All prophetic time-periods have a proportion to one another, and so this common eternity will also have a proportion with them, such that just as a <term>Chronos</term> <note>In the chronological system used by the author, a *Chronus* (or Chronos) represents a specific prophetic unit of time, often calculated as roughly 1,111 years.</note> includes certain times within itself, so eternity includes certain <term>periods of time</term> <note>original: *Chronos*</note> within itself. It is not a single <term>Chronos</term>; three <term>Chroni</term> would be far too many. Thus, it may be 2 <term>Chroni</term>, or 10 periods, or 20 large <term>centuries</term> <note>original: *Secula*</note>, or 2,222 2/3 years. In this way, such an eternity is also longer than the three woes together with the two standstills between them, from the year 510 until 1836, which—even without the standstills—amount to noticeably more than one <term>Chronos</term>, but by no means two <term>Chroni</term>. Furthermore, this eternity is not interrupted like the three woes.

# XIV. 12. Here is—the faith of JESUS.

In Chapter XIII, verse 10, there was a choice to defend oneself, although not without suffering. Now, however, nothing remains but patience; and this is indeed found among the saints. For them, the warning of the third angel has a particularly powerful effect.

¶ **Keep)** <note>original: "Bewahren."</note> This means more than many who came before them.

CII. 19, following the numbering in many German and Latin Bibles of the time; in modern English Bibles, this is Psalm 102:18.</note> and Jeremiah 22:30. ## And I saw — Sickle. XIV. 14.

<meta>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing from the previous page's discussion of the end times.</meta>

Humanity visibly grows toward ripening and maturity.

¶ (A white cloud) The white color of the cloud is a sign of divine grace; the cloud itself is a sign of heavenly power.

¶ (and sitting upon the cloud one like a Son of Man) Here a created angel is described, as also in verses 15, 17, and 18, where it always says, "another angel." Thus, the angels are very busy here. This one with the sickle, and afterwards the angel with the pruning hook <note>original: "Hape"</note>, have a similar task and are of the same kind; yet the first is more noble than the other. Both stand under Jesus Christ, who is Lord of both the harvest and the autumn <note>In this context, "autumn" (Herbst) refers specifically to the grape harvest or vintage, which follows the grain harvest.</note>: and if He Himself were arranging the harvest here, then the autumn vintage would not afterwards be assigned to an angel. An angel can indeed sit upon a cloud, cf. Chapter 10:1, 11:12, 1 Thessalonians 4:17, and can have the form of a man or "Son of Man," as well as a golden crown. Cf. Chapter 4:4, 7.

¶ **Up to the horses' bridles)** This indicates the depth, just as the 1,600 stadia indicates the length of the stream of blood. ¶ **One thousand six hundred stadia far)** In ancient times, 46 ⅔ <term>stadia</term> <note>An ancient Greek unit of distance, roughly 607 feet or 185 meters</note> made one <term>German mile</term> <note>The historical "German mile" was much longer than a modern English mile, equivalent to about 4.6 statute miles or 7.5 kilometers</note>, and later, from the time of Hadrian <note>Roman Emperor, 117–138 AD</note>, 33 stadia were equal to one German mile. As noted by E. Schmid <note>Erasmus Schmid (1570–1637), a noted Lutheran scholar and philologist</note> in his work on the New Testament, page 633. Thus, 1,600 stadia would be over 34 or 48 German miles. The land of Israel does not extend quite that far in length. However, because Jerusalem lies toward the center of the country, the stream of blood in the terrible harvest described here will go far beyond the borders of the land. Oh, what a great slaughter! Another follows in Chapter XIX, verse 21.

¶ **Great and marvelous)** not only great as in Chapter XII, verse 1, but also **marvelous**. This is a progression <note>original: "Gradation," a rhetorical term for a step-by-step increase in intensity or importance</note>.

# And they — have been [made manifest]. XV. 3. 4.

In the Psalms, during thanksgivings for both his terrible and his salvific works, the phrase "for his goodness endures forever" appears often; and this very clause was quite standard in the Israelite worship <note>German: Gottesdienst</note>. 1 Chronicles 17 (16):34; Jeremiah 33:11. Because of this, no one should take offense at the wrath of God and its fulfillment.

¶ For all the nations shall come and worship before you) They will worship you, as their King, in submission and with joy. This is a glorious testimony of the still-impending conversion of all the Gentiles <note>German: Heiden</note>, as the great judgments of God upon the enemies will stir a general sensation among them. Isaiah 25:1, 2, 3; the whole of Psalm 72. Right now, Christendom is a small flock compared to the multitude of those who do not worship the **LORD**. But they shall yet worship him. See also Chapter 11:13; 20:3.

<header>XVI. 1. And — upon the earth.</header>

¶ **No one**) Not only the seven angels to whom the bowls had been given, but also others before them had gone out: see Chapter 14:15, 17. Indeed, the temple was now completely empty of those who otherwise served within it.

Therefore, the angels—having already received the bowls—receive the command to pour them out all together: Chapter 16:1.

812] XVI. 1. And — upon the earth.

2. For the sake of the bowls, one must not restrict the trumpets to such a narrow time as the defenders of the 24-hour day <note>Those who interpret the "days" mentioned in prophecy as literal 24-hour periods.</note> commonly do; and for the sake of the trumpets, one must not extend the bowls as far as the defenders of the year-day <note>original: "jährigen Tages"; the historicist interpretation where one prophetic "day" equals one calendar year.</note> sometimes do.

3. The trumpets concern the kingdom of the world; the bowls concern—largely in that same order—primarily the **Beast**, seeing as it has clothed itself in worldly power.

4. The trumpets passed over the third part of the earth, etc., but the bowls concern the whole and strike much harder. They are concentrated; and even if "the earth" primarily signifies Asia, and "the sea" Europe, etc., it is still to be considered that here, by synecdoche <note>original: *per Synecdochen*; a figure of speech where a part represents the whole, such as using "wheels" to refer to a "car."</note>, the whole earth, the whole sea, all the rivers, etc., are to be understood.

### Verse 2.

> And the first went forth and poured out his bowl upon the earth: and there came a foul sore upon the people who had the mark of the beast, and those who worshipped his image.

¶ **Went forth**) To all seven it was said, "Go your ways": and only regarding this first one is it now said, "he went forth." Did the others not also go forth? ### XVI. 2. And the — worshipped [the] image.
<meta>catchword: The</meta>

¶ **A foul sore**) as in Egypt, **Exodus** 9:9, 10, 11. <note>original: "2 Mos. IX. 9. 10. 11"; the author refers to the Second Book of Moses, known in English as Exodus.</note> Under the **trumpet** of the first **angel** there was a fire, Chapter 8:7, and under the **bowl** of the first **angel** there is a burning pain.

¶ **To the people who etc.**) to these alone, and to all of them.

¶ **The mark**) This **mark** does not yet exist, and consequently even the first **angel** has not yet poured out his **bowl**.

2. Because the pouring out of all seven **bowls** is still in the future, the interpretation of this chapter will be all the shorter.

3. In these **plagues**, the language is much more literal <note>original: "eigentlicher"; meaning the words should be taken at face value rather than as metaphors.</note> than before. Under the **trumpets**, much is figurative <note>original: "verblümt"; literally "flowery" or veiled in metaphors.</note>; for the length of those eras does not permit the literal meaning of the words. But under the **bowls**, things proceed sharply and swiftly. Therefore, they are to be understood much more according to the letter. It is precisely through the literal fulfillment of the **bowls** that the similar-sounding but figuratively-understood expressions under the **trumpets**—which served as preliminary allusions and warnings—are justified. There, the **wrath of God** <note>original: "Grimm GOttes"</note> stirs until it is completed in the **bowls**. One rightly objects to those who weaken the ancient miraculous stories in Holy Scripture through weak interpretations; however, we must just as much fear diminishing the yet-to-come **miraculous deeds** of God.

# And the — in the sea. XVI. 3.

### Verse 3

> And the second [angel] poured out his bowl into the sea; and it became blood as of a dead man: and every living soul died in the sea.

¶ **In the sea**) That here not only the water itself is to be understood, in contrast to the dry land, is clear from the fact that this angel also pours his bowl onto the earth <note>The author refers back to Verse 1, where the command is given to pour the bowls "upon the earth" generally.</note>. v. 1. Thus, the sea is **Europe**; those who are found upon ships are not excluded.

¶ **Blood as of a dead man**) Under the trumpet of the second angel, a similar event occurred involving blood and death. Chapter 8:8, 9. The blood of a dead person is thick and corrupted. How long the sea will remain in this state, the outcome will show.

¶ **Every living soul**) Humans, animals, fish.

<header>XVI. 8. 9. And to — give.</header>

¶ **To him)** meaning the angel. In the Greek <note>original: *autō* (αὐτῷ)</note>, this little word "him" could also be understood as referring to the sun (as in Old German, "the sun" was treated as a masculine noun); however, it is more appropriate for something to be "given" to an angel than to the sun. To the angel it was given (Chapter 15:7) to make humanity hot, not only through the increased heat of the sun, but also through other means of fire. In this manner, the four elements—earth, water, fire, and air—are all afflicted by the bowls of wrath.

¶ **Humanity)** namely the godless, who were meant to perform <term>repentance<note>From the German *Busse*, referring to a turning away from sin and a return to God.</note></term>. Verse 9. This plague, and the others, spread very widely. At that time, there will likely be very few righteous people left on earth, and God will know how to spare them, just as He spared the Israelites in Egypt.

¶ **To scorch them)** Just as there has already been uncommonly great cold once or twice in this century, so a great heat will come in its own time. God has plenty of supply in His storehouses; one occasionally sees evidence of this in the many "fiery phenomena" <note>likely referring to astronomical events like comets or aurorae, seen as portents</note> in the heavens.

**Verse 9. And they blasphemed)** Amid great pain, the weak wish that they themselves did not exist; the wicked, however, break out in rebellion against God.

2. Under the bowls of the previous angels, God is praised in His sanctuary; under the bowls of this and other angels, He and His name are blasphemed by men (verses 11, 21), even though they should instead have penitently given Him the glory.

->Verse 17<-

> **And the seventh poured out his bowl into the air: and there came a great voice out of the temple from the throne, saying: It is done.**

¶ **The seventh**) This angel possesses the most significant bowl of all: and thus this bowl may well require more time to be fulfilled than the bowls of the previous angels.

¶ **Into the air**) There is a great similarity between the <term>trumpets</term> <note>The seven trumpet judgments found in Revelation 8–11.</note> and the <term>bowls</term> <note>The seven bowls of wrath in Revelation 15–16; the author views them as parallel cycles of judgment.</note>, in that both proceed one after another upon the earth, the sea, and so on. But does the trumpet of the seventh angel also concern the air? Answer: although the air is not explicitly mentioned there, the same phenomena occur as here with the bowl poured into the air—namely lightning, voices, thunder, earthquakes, and hail—in all of which the air plays a major part. It is precisely here that the trumpet of the seventh angel and the bowl of the seventh angel converge: (see the final note regarding **Chapter XI. 19.**) and just as that same trumpet, along with the **third woe**, brings much good with it: so this bowl, along with the greatest plague, also carries this purpose: that the earth is brought into a form suitable for the good things that are to follow afterward.

# And—ten horns. XVII. 3.

¶ **In the Spirit**) Thus John remained personally in his place <note>The author suggests that while John's spirit was transported into the vision, his physical body remained stationary.</note>.

¶ **A woman**) Under such an image, both in Scripture and elsewhere, great cities and powers are often represented. Here, an important distinction must be noted: John sees the great city of Babylon under the image of a wanton woman <note>original: "geilen Weibes"; here meaning a woman of loose morals or a harlot</note>; but the Bride, the Wife of the Lamb, is shown to him under the image of a city. On both sides, one must look through the image to that which is depicted—namely, the city of Babylon itself, and the citizens of the New Jerusalem. Yet, in both cases, the city provides the name. New Jerusalem is always called the "Wife of the Lamb" or the "Bride"; but Babylon is often called merely "the woman," because she has no lawful husband, but is instead a harlot.

¶ **Sitting on a scarlet beast**) This beast is the very same one described in Chapter 13. There, it was described alone, as it raged on its own; but now it is described together with the harlot. Both have a very close connection with one another: the seven heads of the beast are seven mountains upon which the woman sits, and they are seven kings (verses 9, 10). Yet both are also notably distinct from one another, although we are generally not accustomed to considering the great difference between the <term>papal power<note>original: päbstlichen Macht</note></term> and the city of Rome. ### And—ten horns. XVII. 3 [845]

...Albericus <note>Alberic II of Spoleto (909–954), who ruled Rome as a dictator</note> incited the Romans, and they gradually developed a desire to restore the old form of their **Republic**, and thus their freedom and glory. At times they behaved in an imperial manner, at times in a clerical one, and in the year **1142** they broke out completely, excluding **Innocent II** from the government and decreeing a Senate which was to stand under a **Patrician** <note>original: "Patricio"; a high-ranking title of nobility</note>, along with several judges. This very thing was the second **symptom** <note>original: "Symptoma"</note> of the deadly wound which we saw in **Chapter XIII. 3**. They continued this game through many fluctuations; yet finally, **Boniface IX** gained complete supremacy in the year **1399**. Since his reign, the city has been kept in check by the **Castel Sant'Angelo** <note>original: "Castell S. Angelo"; the massive fortress in Rome originally built as Hadrian's tomb</note>.

Once the Pope’s power had reached its peak in this regard, the so-called Apostolic Chamber was instead exhausted by the **nepotism** <note>original: "Nepotismum"; the practice of Popes granting wealth and titles to their own relatives</note> introduced soon after. The money that flowed there from the entire Christian world was transferred to families—especially Roman ones—belonging to one Pope or another. This **nerve** <note>original: "Nervus"; referring to the *nervus rerum* or "sinews of power," meaning concentrated wealth</note> can, in its time, do the city great service. The **jealousy** <note>original: "Jalousie"; meaning the rivalry or political envy</note> of the great nobles in Rome against the Pope’s worldly jurisdiction continues on, just as the cruel assault which struck not so much the Romans but rather the Pope himself in the year **1527** <note>The Sack of Rome by the troops of Emperor Charles V</note> arose primarily from this cause. One may read of this very well in **Paolo Giovio’s *Life of Cardinal Pompeo Colonna*** <note>original: "Paulus Jovius in vita Pompeji Columnae cardinalis"</note>.

# XVII. 9. 10. Here is — to remain.
->T. I.<-

¶ **Heads**) We usually use the word "heads" <note>German: *Köpfe*</note> for animals: but in this place, the word "Heads" <note>German: *Häupter*</note> is closer to the original text, because "the five," "the one," and "the other" are in the <term>masculine gender<gloss>original: masculino</gloss></term> and refer to the kings rather than the anatomical heads.

2. In Chapter 13, only a single head was specifically mentioned—namely the first—but here the others are also described in their distinction.

3. Regarding the Beast, the horns, the waters, and the Woman, the text says, "which you saw" (verses 8, 12, 15, 16, 18). This is because the Woman is distinct from the horns and the Beast (as seen when looking back at the verses just cited), the horns and the Beast are distinct from the waters, the waters from the horns, and these from the Beast. Only regarding the heads does it not specifically say "which you saw," because they essentially belong to the Beast itself.

¶ **They are seven mountains, on which the Woman sits, and they are seven kings**) When Rome began to count not just one or another, but seven mountains, there were several small hills among them. However, as it expanded its surrounding walls, every two or even three of the former mountains were counted as one; others—sometimes this one, sometimes that one—were added to the count, thus maintaining the number seven. <note>original: "vid. Gruteri Lampad."; see Janus Gruter's *Lampas*, a famous 17th-century collection of scholarly critiques</note>

# XVII. 9. 10. Here is — to remain.

->Vol. I. page 798.<- *Martinius's Lexicon* <note>Matthias Martinius, author of a famous 17th-century etymological dictionary</note> columns 3174, 3564. Most have since ancient times counted the mountains called the *Aventine*, *Capitoline*, *Caelian*, *Esquiline*, *Palatine*, *Quirinal*, and *Viminal*: and these were fortified and adorned with seven castles or palaces. However, the prophecy does not point specifically to these, but—*without the definite article* <note>original Latin: *absque articulo*</note>—to seven mountains upon which the Woman actually sits at the time when the Beast, and especially she herself in the midst of it, reigns. Now, the *Palatine Hill* has long been uninhabited, a wasteland, and largely a vineyard; on the other hand, the *Vatican Hill* is already counted among the seven in the ancient *Scholia on Juvenal* <note>ancient explanatory notes on the works of the Roman satirist Juvenal</note> and is famous throughout the world for its incomparable preeminence. See *Paolo Aringhi, Volume I, Underground Rome, pages 133, 139.* <note>original Latin: *Pauli Aringhi Tom. I. Rom. subterran.*; a reference to a 1651 work on the catacombs and sacred sites of Rome</note> Regarding most of the others, the situation remains the same. On the *Caelian Hill* stands the Lateran, and on the *Esquiline Hill* St. Mary Major <note>original: *S. Maria Maggiore*</note>: these, together with the *Vatican* and *Quirinal*, which retain their names as mountains, are so many dwellings, churches, or palaces where the papal governments have long found—and even now find—more than enough to occupy themselves, until the remaining mountains fully rise to prominence.

# XVII. 9. 10. Here is—to remain.

...certainly not a skillful interpretation when one assigns two entirely different meanings to a single *symbol* or image. Each head on the beast has only one single meaning, but the thing signified is, in a sense, a *composite* <note>original Latin: *Compositum*</note>, which is made up of a mountain and, upon and with that mountain, a king. *Cluverus* <note>Johannes Cluverus (1593–1633), a German historian and theologian</note> comes quite close to the matter when he writes:

For example, the head of France is *Paris* and the king, etc. *in Commentary on Revelation XVII. p. 238.* <note>original: *in Ap. XVII. f. 238.*</note>

Compare the passage in *Isaiah VII. 8, 9.* <note>original: *Jes. VII. 8. 9.* In this verse, the "head" of Syria is Damascus and the "head" of Damascus is its king, Rezin.</note> Thus, the first head is the first mountain, and upon or with it, the first king; the second head is the second mountain, and also upon or with it, the second king, and so on. The beast has the closest connection not only with the Woman, who sits on the beast for a time, but also with the seven mountains on which the Woman also sits. The mountains are not set down merely as a pure identifying mark of this Woman or of this city, *Rome*—which is otherwise quite clearly designated in the prophecy <note>original: *Weissagung*</note>—but they signify much more. ...and not reported as the Woman’s heads, along with the shared description of the Woman and the Beast; consequently, the kings are not bound exactly to the city or to the mountains of the city alone. However, the mountains of the city and the kings have a very close connection with one another, and each head must signify both a specific king and a specific mountain. No interpreter, no matter how he might try, will likely succeed in explaining the mountains separately from the kings. But by means of the mountains, the kings are distinguished from one another; by means of the kings, the mountains are identified. One might point out seven mountains in Jerusalem, Constantinople, or wherever else one looks. In Rome, on the other hand, from its founding until this very day, one could point out many such mountains <note>The author refers to the famous seven hills of Rome, noting that the city's topography has changed over time</note>, and the Beast may occasionally reside on a level plain in Rome, or even outside the city altogether. Thus, we are to understand here those specific mountains that are occupied by kings, and those kings who established their presence and rule on the mountains of Rome one after another. The relationship between the Beast and the Woman is the main point <note>original: *Haupt=Sache*</note> in this consideration, and one must not be swayed by any seemingly secondary circumstances.

->3. 3<-

# XVII. 9. 10. Here is—to remain.

3. The ten horns that the Beast has are kings; and its seven heads are also called kings this one time. No one will ever be able to demonstrate the true distinction between both the horns and the heads in any purely secular power connected with Rome; but in the Papacy, they can and will indeed be found quite clearly. The heads in their succession, one after another, are the Beast’s own proper parts, belonging to its entire essence. The horns, however, are worldly kings who side with that same Beast during its final period. Therefore, what is stated in verse 17 is reported specifically about the horns as something quite marvelous, namely because the horns—unlike the heads—are otherwise something foreign to the Beast <note>The author suggests that while the "heads" are an intrinsic part of the institution's structure, the "horns" represent external secular powers that choose to lend their strength to it later</note>.

4. The seven heads that the Beast has during its long duration cannot be seven Popes by themselves at different times one after another; for otherwise, the Beast would be without a head for most of its existence, even though it has a continuous government and its previously appointed administration even during a vacant see <note>original: *vacante Sede*; the period when the papal throne is empty between the death of one pope and the election of the next</note>. Nor are they seven papal governments existing alongside one another; for this would be contrary to history <note>original: *Hiſtorie*</note>, as there have never been more than three, and only occasionally two, Popes existing alongside and against one another, one of whom always prevailed over the other. Furthermore, it would partly contradict the text itself, which says: The five have fallen—

v. 10. **The five are fallen**) These ones, together with their mountains and as many heads—insofar as they extend from Gregory VII <note>Pope Gregory VII (reigned 1073–1085), a key figure in the Investiture Controversy who greatly expanded papal power over secular rulers</note> to the present time—we wish to set down here. ...kings emerge so clearly. We provide the following explanation for this.

I. On the Caelian Hill <note>original: *Monte Cœlio*. One of the seven hills of Rome, south of the Esquiline.</note> stands the Lateran <note>original: *Lateranum*. The Lateran Palace was the primary residence of the Popes for about a thousand years, until the Papacy moved to Avignon in 1309.</note>, and that has been the residence of the Roman bishops since the time of the first Christian emperors. Gregory VII <note>Pope Gregory VII (r. 1073–1085), also known as Hildebrand, was a central figure in the medieval struggle between the Church and the Holy Roman Empire.</note> consequently resided there, and he rested as little after he rose to power as did his successors; and although he had to die in Salerno, his successors nevertheless carried on in Rome, and also in the Lateran. From that same time onward, the ecumenical councils <note>original: *Concilia œcumenica*. These are gatherings of high-ranking church officials to decide on matters of doctrine and law.</note>, which had previously all been held in the East <note>original: *Orient*</note>, were held only in the West <note>original: *Occident*</note>—partly indeed for the defense of the truth, but partly also for the suppression of its witnesses, and for the elevation and consolidation of the papal rule, not to mention the many lesser synods <note>original: *Synodorum*</note>. Mostly in Rome, and specifically in the Lateran, four general <note>original: *generalia*</note> and just as many provincial <note>original: *provincialia*</note> councils were held. On this first head was the deadly wound that was healed <note>A reference to Revelation 13:3. The author interprets the historical destruction of the Lateran area as the "wound" to the mountain/head.</note>: and this occurred primarily with the king, but in its measure also with the hill. For in the year 1080, this area of the city was so devastated by Gregory's own party <note>Referring to the conflicts during the Investiture Controversy, specifically the siege of Rome by Emperor Henry IV and the subsequent destructive rescue of Gregory by the Normans.</note> that his successors <note>original: *Successores*</note> could only reoccupy the Lateran a considerable time later.

The ancient palace of the Popes near the Caelian Hill.</note> was in great decay, he relocated to the *Vatican Hill*, which was situated much more advantageously for him against the Romans. For this is still the actual papal residence, grandly fortified since the reign of Boniface IX by the Castel Sant'Angelo <note>original: *Engelsburg*; the "Castle of the Holy Angel," a fortress and palace in Rome</note>.

III. On Monte Cavallo or the Quirinal Hill, the Pope has had his retreat <note>original: *Mutatorium*; a place for changing or a seasonal residence</note> for a long time. The Church of St. Mark stands there, and it was repaired by Paul II, who had previously been the Cardinal-Priest of the title of St. Mark. Alongside it, he built a beautiful palace in which he and his successors, especially in summer, have liked to stay from time to time. On this mountain, Gregory XIII bought a plot of land from the Cardinal of Este and laid out the new Quirinal. Since then, it has once again become the residence of the Popes, most of all when the heat is at its greatest and it is quite unhealthy in the Vatican. For this reason, since the end of the 16th century, much has been dispatched from there, especially concerning the Council of Trent <note>original: *Concilium Tridentinum*; the major reform council of the Catholic Church held between 1545 and 1563</note>. The Inquisition also tends to hold its congregations <note>official committee meetings</note> primarily there.

IV. Where the Esquiline Hill <note>original: *Mons Exquilinus*</note> is at its highest, there stands the noble church of Santa Maria Maggiore. In earlier times, Nicholas IV, Gregory XI, and Martin V were found there as a sort of prelude; but Paul V spent much more of his time there, and since his reign almost everything is handled at Santa Maria Maggiore. In no Roman history, from **Romulus** <note>The legendary founder of Rome</note> to **Gregory VII** <note>Pope Gregory VII (reigned 1073–1085), a key figure in the medieval struggle between church and state</note>, will one encounter a government moving about the hills of Rome in such a way as has occurred since **Gregory VII**. ...since it is so, the difference between the kings may not appear so obvious: but for that very reason, one must not demand too great a difference, but rather stick to the mountains <note>The "seven mountains" mentioned in Revelation 17:9, traditionally identified with the seven hills of Rome</note>, and remember that this is, after all, only a single *Beast* <note>The "Beast" from the Book of Revelation, interpreted here as a continuous historical institution</note>. 7. Finally, it is said of the five together, *They are fallen*. Kings and Popes fall and pass away one after another, and what one does and decrees according to his own particular pleasure is often overturned by his successors. But the main matter, the main purpose, and the main means are always the same, and every Pope fits himself into the time when it is his turn to rule, though some do so less and others more. What **Gregory VII** <note>Pope Gregory VII (reigned 1073–1085), who significantly expanded papal power over secular rulers</note> recently introduced has not been revoked by any successor, no matter how different, up to now (even if he himself might have regretted it before his death). **John XXIII** <note>The Pisan Antipope John XXIII (active 1410–1415)</note> published the *Clementines* <note>original: *Clementinas*; a collection of decretals or church laws named after Pope Clement V</note>, even though **Clement V** <note>Pope Clement V (reigned 1305–1314)</note> himself had commanded their destruction in his final moments. As power-hungry as **Gregory VII** was, so little did **Orsini** <note>Pietro Francesco Orsini, who became Pope Benedict XIII</note> desire to govern an inherited principality; and yet, as **Benedict XIII** <note>Pope Benedict XIII (reigned 1724–1730)</note>, he spoke so very well of what the former had done in his hagiography <note>original: *Legende*; referring to the "Legend" of Gregory VII in the Roman Breviary, which Benedict XIII extended to the whole church, much to the annoyance of secular monarchs</note>.

The Hildebrandine Papacy <note>Refers to the era of papal history beginning with Gregory VII (born Hildebrand), characterized by the assertion of legal and political supremacy over secular rulers</note> is, despite all its fluctuations, such a continuous power that it is called something quite different than the Roman Bishopric was before Gregory VII. The wound from the sword <note>A reference to Revelation 13:3, where one of the heads of the beast is wounded but healed</note>, the voice of the Reformation, the vial of the fifth angel <note>In Revelation 16:10, the fifth vial is poured out upon the "seat of the beast," causing darkness in his kingdom</note>, and the "non-existence" <note>original Latin: *Non-esse*; referring to the Beast that "was, and is not" in Revelation 17:8</note> of the Beast itself, do not mean that its long-standing power, or its even longer duration, has been interrupted. A secular king, before he comes to rule, may have a great reputation, and during his reign encounter very adverse events: nevertheless, only the years of his reign are counted, and these are counted straight through. The five kings stand together in their decrees, which they mostly make upon those five mountains; otherwise, there would be the same difference between the fifth and the others as there is between them and the one that follows. But one should see whether everything they have piled up one after another in such a fashion will not fall together in a heap, and the Beast's dominion on the five mountains be annihilated. The power of those beasts in Daniel 7:12 is likewise ended together.

### Here is — to remain. XVII. 9. 10.

Here, regarding the five kings, the two that remain are very different in their nature. These two also have a type of "remaining" or duration that is distinct from the fifth king. For the first of these two, this duration is quite significant because of how it contrasts with the other; for the second, the duration is short. The former occurs under the dominion of Babylon <note>In apocalyptic literature, "Babylon" is frequently used as a symbol for a corrupt religious or worldly power, often identified with Rome by Reformation-era commentators</note>; the latter occurs during the final, abyssal raging of the Beast.

2. In the second section, both statements can coexist: *The Beast is not; the one is.* This small word, "is," refers only to the time that is present for this second section. For although this one king is powerless, he has not yet passed away. If he did not exist at all, the continuous duration of the Beast—from its rise out of the sea until its plunge into the lake of fire—would be entirely interrupted. The Beast is no longer as it once was, but it has not yet gone into perdition <note>Referring to the description in Revelation 17:8 of the beast that "was, and is not; and shall ascend out of the bottomless pit, and go into perdition."</note>. The "one king" does not stand as the previous five did before their fall; he exists in the state possible during the previously mentioned "non-existence" <note>original Latin: *Non-esse*</note> of the Beast. The sequence and succession <term>Succession: the formal sequence of one person following another in an office</term> of the Popes will not entirely cease during this time. There may well be many, and perhaps even long, vacancies of the See <note>original Latin: *Vacantias Sedis*; the period when a bishop's or pope's office is unoccupied</note> and various disputes.

### XVII. 9. 10. Here is — to remain

[...The power...] has mostly been around this mountain, and upon it the Roman lords conduct their administration <term>Policey: In the 18th century, this term referred to general civil administration, social order, and public governance rather than just modern law enforcement</term>, under the yoke, quite insignificantly until now. However, their so-called *Conservatores* <note>original: "Conservators"; these were municipal magistrates in Rome who represented the city's ancient civil authority</note> serve for the preservation and continuation of the same, until the woman shall swing herself up upon the Beast. Whenever there is a papal death, the Capitoline Hill <note>original: *Capitolium*</note> makes itself heard by means of a bell hanging there, which is otherwise never rung. Also, the Roman Senate has already attained a much greater distinction through Innocent XI and, as previously mentioned, through Clement XII <note>Pope Innocent XI (reigned 1676–1689) and Pope Clement XII (reigned 1730–1740) were known for various administrative and architectural reforms in Rome</note>, than it had previously possessed. For the other king, the Viminal Hill <note>original Latin: *Mons Viminalis*</note> presumably remains.

**Woman—City)** In a positive sense, these two designations also appear together in Chapter 21, verses 2, 9, and 10. <note>In Chapter 21, the "Woman" is the Bride/New Jerusalem, whereas here in Chapter 17, the Woman is the Harlot/Babylon.</note>

¶ **Over the kings of the earth)** Thus, it is a very high and extensive power that is attributed to this queen.

## XVIII. 14. And — find no more.

**Jerome** <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the primary translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible.</note> calls them **Italian carriages** <note>original: "rhedas Italiae"</note> in **Isaiah 66:20**. Thus, this word points toward the Latins or Italians: for whose sake we have used the word **coach** <note>original: "Carrozza," an early modern loanword in German from Italian.</note> in our translation.

¶ **And bondmen, and slaves.** Actually: **bodies**, and **human souls**; and both usually have the same meaning. But here there are two different **grammatical cases** in the Greek. The horses and carriages and **bodies** stand together, and thus the "bodies" are those slaves who, like cattle, are used to carry, lead, or drag other goods. Consequently, the "**human souls**" are those slaves who are bought and sold themselves, or who are kept for services other than those mentioned before. <note>The author suggests a distinction between "bodies" as pack-animals/laborers and "souls" as domestic or specialized slaves.</note>

That very voice, which introduces the kings and merchants as speakers, also interjects this itself at a very appropriate place.

<header>And to the—Hallelujah. XIX. 3. 4.</header>

### Verse 3.

> And a second time they said: **Hallelujah**; and her smoke rises up forever and ever.

¶ **A second time**) The first time they said **Hallelujah** because the judgment had now taken place; and the second time they say **Hallelujah** in contemplation of the **eternity** of such a judgment.

¶ **And her smoke**) The little word *and* links this speech and the end of verse 2 closely together. The **Hallelujah** is spoken both times by one [choir], and the remaining **song of praise** by another choir, one after the other. Compare **Chapter XV. 4.** <note>This refers to antiphonal singing, a practice where two parts of a choir respond to one another, common in both ancient Hebrew and early Christian worship.</note>

2. The smoke of the **burning** is mentioned in **Chapter XVIII. 9, 18.** But even when the flame and the burning are over, the smoke will continue until the first earth passes away. That may be called a **ban**! <term>Ban: derived from the German *Bann* (similar to the Hebrew *herem*), referring to something or someone devoted to total destruction or excluded from the community under a divine curse.</term> In the meantime, it is in that sense not yet an eternal smoke; but from the torment of those who helped with the works of the great **Whore**, the smoke will rise eternally. Compare **Chapter XIV. 11.** And thus the smoke of **Babylon** and the smoke from the **Lake of Fire** will rise up together.

### Verse 4.

> And the twenty-four elders and the four living creatures <note>original: *Thiere* (beasts). In modern English Bibles, these are usually called "living creatures," representing all of creation or specific heavenly attendants.</note> fell down and worshiped **God**, who sat on the throne, and said: **Amen Hallelujah**.

<header>XIX. 5. And — the Great ones.</header>

¶ **And the)** The four living creatures <note>original: *Thiere* (beasts). Referring to the "four living creatures" described in Revelation 4, which represent the highest order of created beings surrounding God's throne.</note> are closer to the throne than the 24 elders: and in Chapter IV. 9, 10 and V. 8, 14, they are mentioned before the elders regarding the praise they bring, because in those instances the movement goes from the Center <note>original: *Centro*</note> to the Circumference <note>original: *Umkreis*</note>. Here, however, since the judgments are fulfilled, the movement returns from the circumference back to the center, and for that reason the elders are named first.

¶ **Amen)** With this, they join in the song of praise found in verses 1, 2, and 3. A similar **Amen** is spoken by the four living creatures in Chapter V. 14, and by all the angels in Chapter VII. 12.

### Verse 5.

> And a voice went out from the throne, which said: Praise our God, all his servants, and you who fear him, both the small and the great.

¶ **A voice)** This voice is not God's own, for it says: **Our God.** And yet it proceeds from the throne; it may therefore well be attributed to the four living creatures.

¶ **Praise)** The reason and the content of this praise follows immediately hereafter in verse 6, etc. In verses 1–4, there were songs of praise over the judgment of the great Whore; now there are songs of praise over what follows further, as the LORD God, the Almighty, takes up the kingdom or the government and subdues the remaining enemies.

¶ **All)** Not only those mentioned in the 2nd verse.

## Verse 17.

> And I saw an angel standing in the sun; and he cried with a loud voice, saying to all the birds that fly in the midst of heaven: Come and gather yourselves together unto the great supper of **GOD**, 18 that ye may eat the flesh of kings, and the flesh of captains <note>original: "Obristen," referring to high-ranking military commanders or officers.</note>, and the flesh of mighty men, and the flesh of horses and of them that sit on them, and the flesh of all men, both free and bond, both small and great.

### And cast — a little while. XX. 3.

It is not to be assumed that this refers to what is meant in Chapter VI. 11 or X. 6, because this "little <term>Chronos: a Greek word for a duration of time; the author uses it here as a technical term for a specific prophetic period</term>" appears in the latter part of the prophecy. [Introduction, p. 146.] However, that which Satan will do during this little while (verses 8 and 9) does not happen very quickly, and this little <term>Chronos</term> cannot end before the thousand years of the saints begin; the order of the text demands this. 

All time periods <note>original: *Zeitläuffe*</note> from Chapter XII. 12 to the end of the vision have a proportion to one another, as was shown in the Introduction on p. 127; and so the "short time" will not stand apart from them. 

If, for example, one takes 1111 1/9 years—which constitute a full <term>Chronos</term> or period—and subtracts the thousand (similar to the Jewish <term>liphrat katon: Hebrew for "minor era," a method of abbreviating years by omitting the thousands place</term>), then the "short time" and the "little while" enter into such a proportion with each other, first at 888 8/9 and 111 1/9, and following their sum, they reach a complete equality with the 1000 years. 

Since so many time periods are indicated more than once and in different ways in the prophecy, it works out quite well when the single "short time" and the single "little while" relate to each other in a certain proportion. And assuming this, just as the imprisonment of Satan—during which he cannot deceive the nations—lasts a thousand years, so too the deception under the third woe <note>A reference to the "Three Woes" associated with the final trumpet blasts in Revelation</note>, occurring both before and after the imprisonment, together also lasts a thousand years,

## XX. 4. And—a thousand years.

and the space between the fall of Satan into the Lake of Fire and the end of all things would be equal to the "short time" <note>The author refers to the technical duration of time discussed on the previous page</note>. ->Verse 4.<-

### And — a thousand years. XX. 4.

¶ **They)** namely, the saints, whom John saw at the same time. Daniel 7:22.

¶ **A judgment)** Great authority! <note>original: *Gewalt*; in this context, it implies the legal power or jurisdiction to pass judgment</note> 1 Corinthians 6:2.

¶ **To them)** Who these might be, and how many of them there are, is not indicated. They are distinct from those souls who are mentioned immediately afterward, and are thus saints who were already resurrected previously.

¶ **And the souls)** And, namely, I saw the souls, etc. The word "soul" is used here as in Chapter 6:9, and signifies a particular class of the dead, to whom "the rest of the dead" are contrasted by their later coming to life in verse 5.

¶ **Executed with the ax)** In the Old and New Testaments, the sword is often mentioned, but in this single passage, the ax is noted. This points toward Rome, where it was customary to use the ax, <term>Securis <note>original: "Securis"; the traditional Roman executioner's ax</note></term>, to execute both criminals and martyrs, and where it was convenient to finish off many at once. However, those martyrs are by no means excluded who, in ancient or modern times, were executed in another even more cruel manner than by the ax, in Rome and other Roman-minded places, for the sake of the testimony of Jesus, etc., before the times of the Beast, and during the times of the Beast and his image and mark.

#### [Header: The rest — Resurrection]

is placed only for the sake of elegance, but actually corresponds quite precisely with the matter itself, since the **rest from the dead are** the remaining part of the whole multitude of the dead, or of all those who have not yet attained immortality. See verse 12.

### The Rest of—Resurrection. XX. 5.

The current unbelieving rabble of those who despise God conducts itself partly so crudely and partly so subtly that one might doubt whether the Devil himself could take it any further. They must not, however, imagine that they possess any special—even if false—cleverness, let alone that they have brought their cause to its peak or would do so soon. They are merely beginners; the true master-scoffers are not yet born. These future scoffers will turn the coming rich measure of light into error and, in the end, be most powerfully put to shame. 

Meanwhile, just as one gives such miserable people a great advantage when one sets the end of the world too near—since they believe they have "won" when that end unexpectedly fails to appear—they can, conversely, achieve nothing when one demonstrates the true length of the world’s remaining duration <term>Welt-Währung: referring to the "currency" or continued existence of the world's current age</term> from the Scriptures. Indeed, the events that must be fulfilled one after another beforehand are proof that the end, which is likewise proclaimed, will come likewise in its own time. Whether a special warning against complacency <note>original: *Sicherheit*; in this context, it refers to a dangerous spiritual apathy or a false sense of safety</note> and mockery, together with a contempt for such warning, will precede the end of the world (just as in the days of Noah), will be seen at that time.

# XX. 10. And—forever and ever.

over a thousand years and a little while besides. <note>The author is quoting the "little season" mentioned in Revelation 20:3, following the thousand-year binding of Satan.</note>
In **2 Thessalonians 2:8**, Paul placed the destruction of the **man of sin** or the **beast** together with the appearance of the coming of Christ; but Revelation now inserts exactly between these two points—which it describes in **Chapter 19:20** and **Chapter 20:11**—that which stands in **Chapter 20:1–10**. In turn, Paul, under divine providence, arranged his words in such a way that this passage could very well be inserted at the proper time. Divine revelations <term>Entdeckungen</term> <note>Literally "discoveries" or "unveilings," here referring to the unfolding of biblical prophecy over time.</note> proceed step by step; and regarding these, one must not misuse that which was first only indicated summarily (consider, for example, **Matthew 24:29** and **26:64**) to destroy or even condemn as heretical <term>verketzern</term> that which is later opened up more fully and circumstantially. Rather, both must be gratefully recognized, one being explained from the other, and most of all—as nature itself teaches—the former being explained from the latter.

When comparing the passage from Paul and the Revelation, this is all the more natural because the destruction <term>Vertilgung</term> of the **man of sin** is an incomparable ray from the appearance of the coming of Jesus Christ. The two millennia <note>original: "zwey Jahr-Tausende." The author appears to be counting the thousand years of the kingdom and perhaps another distinct period, or interpreting the "thousand years" in a specific chronological way characteristic of 18th-century Pietist eschatology.</note> are located between the two great days of glorious vengeance and salvation, the first of which is a model, vanguard, and pledge <note>original: "Angelt," an archaic term for "earnest money" or a down-payment that guarantees a future fulfillment.</note> of the other; just as between the destruction of **Antiochus** <note>Antiochus IV Epiphanes, the Seleucid king whose persecution of the Jews was seen by many theologians as a historical "type" or precursor to the Antichrist.</note>, who was a prototype of the beast, and the destruction of the

Some wish to make the thousand years <note>The Millennium</note> into eternity itself, and others, conversely, wish to place the new heaven and the new earth, along with the New Jerusalem, into the thousand years and thus within the bounds of time. These are, once again, two extremes; and we shall once more remain simply with the text. The thousand years occur before the end of all things; but the new heaven and the new earth, along with the New Jerusalem, belong to the **New All** <note>original: *Neue All*, referring to the restoration of the entire universe or "all things new" in verse 5</note>, or rather, they constitute it themselves (verse 5).

...beloved city be surrounded by Gog and Magog <note>A reference to the final rebellion described in Revelation 20:8</note>, but an almost universal security in unbelief and earthly-mindedness will also prevail upon the earth. 4. Among the ancient prophets, especially in **Isaiah**, there are many expressions regarding the Church of the New Testament which are here attributed to the New Jerusalem (just as Jerusalem is mentioned in connection with the new heaven and the new earth in Isaiah 65:17–18 and 66:20, 22). The reason for this is that they generally grouped together everything that was yet to come, seeing how it is fulfilled both within time—particularly in the end times (Chapter 10:7)—and in eternity (for the New Testament is an *eternal testament*). However, in the prophecy of the New Testament itself, the "presently new" is presupposed, and the focus is directed toward the "yet future new" (cf. Matthew 26:29), namely, toward **eternal well-being**. Thus, the prophecies of the Old Testament are presupposed in the sense of their initial fulfillment, while the sense of the complete, exceedingly glorious fulfillment retains its

The purpose of this book—to show what must happen—in no way forces us to interpret the new heaven and the new earth, along with the New Jerusalem, as referring merely to the Church of the New Testament and the "latter times" <note>a reference to the final period of earthly history before the end of the world</note>.
